    26  Actions by the United States in the 
    27                  Investigations Under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 
    28                  1974 of the Acts, Policies, and Practices of 60 
    29                  Economies Related to the Failure of Each Economy To 
    30                  Impose and Effectively Enforce a Prohibition on the 
    31                  Importation of Goods Produced With Forced Labor
    32  
    33                  Memorandum for the United States Trade Representative
    34  
    35                  On March 12, 2026, the United States Trade 
    36                  Representative (Trade Representative) initiated 
    37                  investigations under section 301 of the Trade Act of 
    38                  1974, as amended (19 U.S.C. 2411) (section 301), into 
    39                  the acts, policies, and practices of 60 economies to 
    40                  examine whether any of the economies subject to these 
    41                  investigations fail to prohibit or to effectively 
    42                  enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods 
    43                  produced wholly or in part with forced labor and 
    44                  whether the failure is unreasonable or discriminatory 
    45                  and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce. 91 Fed. Reg. 
    46                  12884 (Initiation of Section 301 Investigations). The 
    47                  economies subject to these investigations are:
    48  
    49                      1. Algeria
    50                      2. Angola
    51                      3. Argentina
    52                      4. Australia
    53                      5. The Bahamas
    54                      6. Bahrain
    55                      7. Bangladesh
    56                      8. Brazil
    57                      9. Cambodia
    58                      10. Canada
    59                      11. Chile
    60                      12. China, People's Republic of
    61                      13. Colombia
    62                      14. Costa Rica
    63                      15. Dominican Republic
    64                      16. Ecuador
    65                      17. Egypt
    66                      18. El Salvador
    67                      19. European Union
    68                      20. Guatemala
    69                      21. Guyana
    70                      22. Honduras
    71                      23. Hong Kong, China
    72                      24. India
    73  
    74  [[Page 47718]]
    75  
    76                      25. Indonesia
    77                      26. Iraq
    78                      27. Israel
    79                      28. Japan
    80                      29. Jordan
    81                      30. Kazakhstan
    82                      31. Kuwait
    83                      32. Libya
    84                      33. Malaysia
    85                      34. Mexico
    86                      35. Morocco
    87                      36. New Zealand
    88                      37. Nicaragua
    89                      38. Nigeria
    90                      39. Norway
    91                      40. Oman
    92                      41. Pakistan
    93                      42. Peru
    94                      43. Philippines
    95                      44. Qatar
    96                      45. Russia
    97                      46. Saudi Arabia
    98                      47. Singapore
    99                      48. South Africa
   100                      49. South Korea
   101                      50. Sri Lanka
   102                      51. Switzerland
   103                      52. Taiwan
   104                      53. Thailand
   105                      54. Trinidad and Tobago
   106                      55. T[uuml]rkiye
   107                      56. United Arab Emirates
   108                      57. United Kingdom
   109                      58. Uruguay
   110                      59. Venezuela
   111                      60. Vietnam
   112  
   113                  On June 2, 2026, the Trade Representative determined 
   114                  that the acts, policies, and practices of each of these 
   115                  economies are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. 
   116                  commerce and thus are actionable under section 
   117                  301(b)(1) (19 U.S.C. 2411(b)(1)) (Notice of 
   118                  Determinations: 2026-11296; 91 Fed. Reg. 34272) (Notice 
   119                  of Determinations).
   120  
   121                  As a result of these determinations, the Trade 
   122                  Representative proposed to determine in each 
   123                  investigation that action is appropriate under section 
   124                  301 to obtain the elimination of the actionable acts, 
   125                  policies, and practices, including imposing ad valorem 
   126                  tariffs on all goods of each investigated economy, with 
   127                  exemptions for certain goods. To obtain the elimination
   128  
   129  [[Page 47719]]
   130  
   131                  of the actionable acts, policies, and practices in each 
   132                  investigation, the Trade Representative proposed 
   133                  section 301 tariffs. The Trade Representative proposed 
   134                  tariffs of 10 percent ad valorem on goods of economies 
   135                  that: impose a forced labor import prohibition but do 
   136                  not yet effectively enforce it (Canada, Ecuador, the 
   137                  European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and Pakistan); have 
   138                  undertaken commitments in their respective Agreements 
   139                  on Reciprocal Trade regarding forced labor import 
   140                  prohibitions (Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, 
   141                  El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and 
   142                  Taiwan); or have imposed a partial regime with the 
   143                  effect of preventing the importation of certain forced 
   144                  labor goods (the United Kingdom). For all other 
   145                  economies whose failure to impose forced labor import 
   146                  prohibitions the Trade Representative has found 
   147                  actionable under section 301, the Trade Representative 
   148                  proposed section 301 tariffs of 12.5 percent ad 
   149                  valorem. In addition, the Trade Representative proposed 
   150                  to establish a textile mechanism that would allow a 
   151                  certain volume of apparel and textile imports to enter 
   152                  the United States at a zero section 301 tariff rate.
   153  
   154                  The Office of the United States Trade Representative 
   155                  (USTR) invited comments by interested persons on these 
   156                  proposed actions and convened public hearings on July 
   157                  7, 8, and 9, 2026. USTR received over 1,600 written 
   158                  comments and testimony from over 100 witnesses at the 
   159                  hearings.
   160  
   161                  The Trade Representative has informed me of the 
   162                  substance of significant comments on the proposed 
   163                  actions in each investigation and provided me his 
   164                  advice on appropriate actions, including tariffs of 
   165                  various rates, exemptions for certain products, and 
   166                  tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) for specific types of 
   167                  products for certain economies. For example, the Trade 
   168                  Representative advised me that after considering the 
   169                  comments and testimony received, certain products 
   170                  warrant exemption from tariffs imposed in connection 
   171                  with an investigation, including because of the needs 
   172                  of the U.S. economy or based on the extent to which 
   173                  imposing tariffs on the products will contribute to the 
   174                  elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of the 
   175                  economies found to be actionable in the investigations 
   176                  described above. These exemptions encompass (a) raw 
   177                  materials that if subject to the proposed additional 
   178                  tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic 
   179                  supply; (b) products that could cause economy-wide 
   180                  disruptions if subject to the proposed additional 
   181                  tariffs; (c) products that cannot be grown or produced 
   182                  in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the 
   183                  United States or obtained from other sources; (d) 
   184                  products that if exempted from these tariffs would 
   185                  encourage economies that have made commitments to the 
   186                  United States regarding forced labor import 
   187                  prohibitions to implement those commitments or to enact 
   188                  and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
   189                  prohibition; or (e) articles for which these tariffs 
   190                  may not contribute substantially to the elimination of 
   191                  the acts, policies, and practices of the economies 
   192                  found to be actionable in the investigations described 
   193                  above.
   194  
   195                  The Trade Representative has also advised me that for 
   196                  goods of the European Union, Japan, Korea, Switzerland, 
   197                  or Taiwan, section 301 tariffs that are the net of 
   198                  Most-Favored Nation (MFN) tariffs would be consistent 
   199                  with their respective Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or 
   200                  similar arrangements and would be appropriate to 
   201                  encourage these economies to fulfill commitments 
   202                  regarding forced labor import prohibitions or to enact 
   203                  or effectively enforce such a prohibition.
   204  
   205                  Further, the Trade Representative has advised me that, 
   206                  based on the comments and testimony received, the 
   207                  establishment of TRQs on certain textile and apparel 
   208                  goods is appropriate as a means to encourage the 
   209                  importation by trading partners of U.S. cotton and 
   210                  textile goods, in order to reduce the reliance of such 
   211                  partners on inputs from other sources that are more 
   212                  likely to contain forced labor inputs. Such TRQs, in 
   213                  combination with other tariffs on other products of 
   214                  those trading partners, are appropriate to obtain the 
   215                  elimination of the acts, policies, or practices found 
   216                  actionable under section 301 for those trading 
   217                  partners. The Trade Representative has also
   218  
   219  [[Page 47720]]
   220  
   221                  informed me that establishing these TRQs is not 
   222                  feasible at this time, but that establishing these TRQs 
   223                  will be feasible by September 1, 2026.
   224  
   225                  Finally, the Trade Representative has informed me that 
   226                  following consultation with certain economies in these 
   227                  investigations and publication of the Notice of 
   228                  Determinations, additional economies have imposed 
   229                  forced labor import prohibitions (Cambodia, Guatemala, 
   230                  Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad and Tobago) or 
   231                  undertaken commitments regarding forced labor import 
   232                  prohibitions in an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade 
   233                  (Jordan). As a result of these actions, the Trade 
   234                  Representative has advised me that the goods of these 
   235                  economies should be tariffed at the 10 percent rate to 
   236                  further encourage these economies to effectively 
   237                  enforce such prohibitions, and, in the case of Jordan, 
   238                  to enact and effectively enforce its commitments 
   239                  regarding forced labor import prohibitions.
   240  
   241                  After considering the relevant issues and factors and 
   242                  weighing the relevant considerations, including this 
   243                  information and advice from the Trade Representative; 
   244                  the information, findings, and determinations in USTR's 
   245                  Notice of Determinations; and the need to obtain the 
   246                  elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of the 
   247                  investigated economies found to be actionable under 
   248                  section 301, it is hereby directed as follows:
   249  
   250                  Section 1. Tariffs and Exemptions. (a) Except as 
   251                  otherwise provided in this memorandum, the Trade 
   252                  Representative shall impose the following tariff rates 
   253                  on all goods of the economy for which an act, policy, 
   254                  or practice was found actionable under section 301:
   255  
   256  (i) 10 percent tariff rate: The Trade Representative shall impose a tariff 
   257  of 10 percent on goods of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, 
   258  El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, 
   259  Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the United Kingdom, and Trinidad and Tobago.
   260  
   261  (ii) Tariff rate of 10 percent or 12.5 percent, net of MFN rate: For a 
   262  product of the European Union or Taiwan, where such product's MFN tariff is 
   263  less than 10 percent, the Trade Representative shall impose a section 301 
   264  tariff pursuant to these investigations so that the sum of the MFN tariff 
   265  and the section 301 tariff shall be 10 percent, and where such product's 
   266  MFN tariff is greater than or equal to 10 percent, the Trade Representative 
   267  shall impose a section 301 tariff of zero. For a product of Japan, Korea, 
   268  or Switzerland, where such product's MFN tariff is less than 12.5 percent, 
   269  the Trade Representative shall impose a section 301 tariff pursuant to 
   270  these investigations so that the sum of the MFN tariff and the tariff 
   271  imposed pursuant to these investigations shall be 12.5 percent, and where 
   272  such product's MFN tariff is greater than or equal to 12.5 percent, the 
   273  Trade Representative shall impose a section 301 tariff of zero. Capping 
   274  total duties in this manner is feasible, consistent with the terms of the 
   275  Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or similar arrangements, and appropriate to 
   276  encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor 
   277  import prohibitions or to enact and effectively enforce such a prohibition.
   278  
   279  (iii) 12.5 percent tariff rate: For goods of all other investigated 
   280  economies, the Trade Representative shall impose a tariff rate of 12.5 
   281  percent.
   282  
   283                      (b) The Trade Representative shall exempt from the 
   284                  tariffs imposed as directed in subsection (a) of this 
   285                  section the products identified in the Annex to this 
   286                  memorandum for each economy for which an act, policy, 
   287                  or practice was found actionable under section 301, as 
   288                  the products identified constitute:
   289  
   290  (i) raw materials that if subject to these tariffs could lead to the 
   291  unavailability of domestic supply;
   292  
   293  (ii) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to these 
   294  tariffs;
   295  
   296  (iii) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient quantities in 
   297  the United States or obtained from other sources;
   298  
   299  [[Page 47721]]
   300  
   301  (iv) products for which these tariffs may not be effective in obtaining the 
   302  elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of economies found to be 
   303  actionable in the investigations; or
   304  
   305  (v) certain products of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El 
   306  Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, 
   307  Switzerland, Taiwan, or the United Kingdom that would encourage these 
   308  economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor import prohibitions 
   309  or to encourage these economies to enact and effectively enforce a forced 
   310  labor import prohibition.
   311  
   312                      (c) After considering the relevant issues and 
   313                  factors and weighing the relevant considerations, 
   314                  including potential economic harm and efficacy of 
   315                  tariffs, I determine that the products identified in 
   316                  the Annex to this memorandum shall be exempted from the 
   317                  tariffs directed in subsection (a) of this section, and 
   318                  the Trade Representative shall direct that the 
   319                  Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) 
   320                  be modified as provided in the Annex to this 
   321                  memorandum. In my judgment, the tariffs directed in 
   322                  subsection (a) of this section with the exemptions 
   323                  described in subsection (b) of this section are 
   324                  appropriate and feasible to obtain the elimination of 
   325                  the acts, policies, or practices of the economies found 
   326                  to be actionable under section 301.
   327  
   328                  Sec. 2. Tariff-Rate Quotas. (a) As soon as the Trade 
   329                  Representative determines that it is feasible, the 
   330                  Trade Representative shall:
   331  
   332  (i) establish TRQs for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia, with 
   333  an initial duration of 3 years, to encourage the importation by each of 
   334  these economies of U.S. textile goods, in order to reduce reliance on 
   335  inputs from other sources that are more likely to contain forced labor 
   336  inputs; and
   337  
   338  (ii) structure the TRQs for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia 
   339  to allow for a certain volume of specific textiles and apparel, based on 
   340  that economy's importation of U.S. inputs, to enter the United States free 
   341  of the section 301 tariffs provided for in section 1(a) of this memorandum.
   342  
   343                      (b) As soon as the Trade Representative determines 
   344                  that it is feasible, the Trade Representative shall:
   345  
   346  (i) establish TRQs for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia, with 
   347  an initial duration of 3 years, to encourage the importation by each of 
   348  these economies of U.S. cotton, in order to reduce reliance on inputs from 
   349  other sources that are more likely to contain forced labor inputs; and
   350  
   351  (ii) structure the TRQs for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia 
   352  to allow for a certain volume of specific textile and apparel, based on 
   353  that economy's importation of U.S. cotton, to enter the United States free 
   354  of the section 301 tariffs provided for in section 1(a) of this memorandum.
   355  
   356                      (c) Until the Trade Representative establishes the 
   357                  TRQs described in subsections (a) and (b) of this 
   358                  section, the Trade Representative shall impose the 
   359                  applicable section 301 tariffs provided for in section 
   360                  1(a) of this memorandum (here, 10 percent) on imports 
   361                  of specific textile and apparel of Bangladesh, 
   362                  Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia that will be covered 
   363                  by the TRQs for each of those economies.
   364                      (d) The Trade Representative shall modify the HTSUS 
   365                  as appropriate to implement the directives in this 
   366                  section. The Trade Representative shall publish a 
   367                  notice in the Federal Register regarding the 
   368                  establishment and the effective date of the TRQs 
   369                  directed in this section.
   370                      (e) After considering the relevant issues and 
   371                  factors and weighing the relevant considerations, 
   372                  including potential economic harm and efficacy of 
   373                  tariffs, I determine that the actions directed in this 
   374                  section are appropriate and feasible to obtain the 
   375                  elimination of the applicable economies' acts, 
   376                  policies, or practices found actionable under section 
   377                  301.
   378  
   379  [[Page 47722]]
   380  
   381                  Sec. 3. Additional Explanation. (a) After considering 
   382                  the relevant issues and factors and weighing the 
   383                  relevant considerations, including potential economic 
   384                  harm and efficacy of tariffs, I determine that the 
   385                  actions directed in this memorandum are appropriate and 
   386                  feasible to obtain the elimination of the act, policy, 
   387                  or practice of each economy found to be actionable 
   388                  under section 301.
   389  
   390                      (b) In my judgment, each tariff of 10 percent on 
   391                  all goods of Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and 
   392                  Malaysia, with the exemptions for certain goods as 
   393                  discussed in section 1(b) of this memorandum and the 
   394                  TRQs discussed in section 2 of this memorandum, is 
   395                  appropriate and feasible to obtain the elimination of 
   396                  the acts, policies, or practices of Bangladesh, 
   397                  Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia found to be 
   398                  actionable under section 301.

content.text:
Memorandum says USTR received over 1,600 comments / over 100 witnesses. Statement 2 says over 450 / nearly 60—incorrect. Could be June proposal says something? Need check. Q14 asks statements about action; likely trap: memorandum says 1,600 but perhaps notice says 450? Let's inspect June proposal. Also statement 3 seven economies moved from 12.5 to 10 due to forced labor ban: It says "After June proposal, seven economies were moved..." Actually adopted rate 10 for Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago + Jordan (ART) = seven. Yes correct, but did each adopt forced-labor import ban? Jordan ART, others ban. Could be statement partly correct because India etc. yes. Need check June proposal rates. Likely these seven were 12.5. The memorandum lists "additional economies have imposed ... (Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago) or undertaken commitments ... (Jordan)" and 10%. Correct if "seven economies" means these seven; one by ART not ban. Wording "because each adopted a forced-labor import ban" inaccurate for Jordan. Could be "partly correct."

Statement 4: USTR removed beef and avocados from list of exempt products. Text says determined not to remove these products from list; they remain exempt. So incorrect.
Statement 5: Every economy whose rate is net of MFN also has its own negotiated list of exempt products. Net economies EU, Taiwan, Japan, Korea, Switzerland. Annex II Parts: C EU, K Taiwan, D Switzerland; Japan and Korea no country-specific parts (only Part A). So incorrect: Japan/Korea no separate negotiated list.
Statement 6: 471 more products incl all sugar and sugar-containing products. Text says additional 471 products and "certain sugar and sugar containing products" not all. Partly correct.
Statement 7: USTR stated no product will bear more than 12.5 percent duty in total. Did it? The cap is total MFN + 301 = 10 or 12.5 for net economies, but 12.5 flat economies could have MFN plus 12.5 = >12.5. Maybe statement misreads. Need search exact phrase "no product" / "total". 
Statement 8: FTZ privileged status unless domestic status. Notice text line 489 says exactly. Correct, though wording "once duties apply must be admitted privileged unless eligible domestic" yes.
Statement 9: correct.
Statement 10: Of products on proposal's Annex A, only ones cut back were certain chemicals. Text: "exempt all products proposed ... except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products" and "determined not to remove additional products." So correct. But perhaps also beef/avocados? It says determined not to remove. So only chemicals cut back. Correct.

Statement 1: Memorandum gives USTR until Sept 1? It says establishing TRQs feasible by Sept 1, directs "as soon as determines feasible" and until established impose 10%. No deadline Sept 1. Incorrect. Need exact text.

Now June proposal details. Read key sections: summary, rates, exempt list, comments count? Q14 statement 2 "USTR received over 450 written comments and heard nearly 60 witnesses" maybe June proposal says that? No, proposal before comments. Could be notice says something like over 450 comments received in response to initiation? Let's read full June proposal sections around 1-430.

    24  AGENCY: Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR).

    26  ACTION: Notice of determinations, request for comments, and notice of

    31  SUMMARY: On March 12, 2026, the United States Trade Representative 
    32  (Trade Representative) initiated 60 investigations related to the 
    33  failure of various economies to impose and effectively enforce a 
    34  prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor. The 
    35  Trade Representative has determined that 54 of the investigated 
    36  economies have failed to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor 
    37  import prohibition. The Trade Representative has determined that six of 
    38  the investigated economies have failed to effectively enforce a forced 
    39  labor import prohibition. The Trade Representative has determined that 
    40  the failure of each of the investigated economies to impose and 
    41  effectively enforce a force labor import prohibition is unreasonable 
    42  and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce. As a result of the findings in 
    43  each investigation, the Trade Representative proposes that appropriate 
    44  action includes additional duties on all products of the investigated 
    45  economies, except as provided in Annex A to this Notice. For economies 
    46  that impose a forced labor import prohibition; have taken on 
    47  commitments related to forced labor import prohibitions through an 
    48  Agreement on Reciprocal Trade; or have imposed a partial regime with 
    49  the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods, 
    50  the Trade Representative proposes 10% as the rate of additional duties. 
    51  For all other economies, the Trade Representative proposes 12.5% as the 
    52  rate of additional duties. The Trade Representative also proposes a 
    53  textile mechanism that would allow for a certain volume of apparel and 
    54  textile imports from certain economies to enter the United States at a 
    55  reduced Section 301 tariff rate. USTR seeks public comments on the 
    56  proposed actions in the investigations and will hold public hearings in 
    57  connection with the proposals.

    62  date.

    66  Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, beginning at 10:00 
    67  a.m., and continuing, as appropriate.
    68      Five days after the last day of the public hearings: Submit post-
    69  hearing rebuttal comments.

    71  ADDRESSES: Submit documents in response to this Notice, including 
    72  written comments, rebuttal comments, and requests to appear through 
    73  USTR's electronic portal: https://comments.ustr.gov/s/. The docket 
    74  number for written comments and rebuttal comments is USTR-2026-0265. 
    75  The docket number for requests to appear is USTR-2026-0266.

    77  FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: For procedural questions concerning 
    78  comments, contact the USTR Section 301 support line at (202) 395-5725. 
    79  Direct all other questions regarding this notice to Megan Grimball,

    86      On March 12, 2026, the Trade Representative initiated 60 
    87  investigations related to the failure of various economies to impose

    92  17, 2026). The notice of initiation solicited written comments on, 
    93  inter alia: whether any economy subject to these investigations 
    94  maintains or is in the process of establishing a forced labor import 
    95  prohibition, and whether any such import prohibition is being 
    96  effectively enforced; the extent to which the failure of any economy to 
    97  establish and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition is 
    98  unreasonable, discriminates against U.S. goods, or constitutes a 
    99  persistent pattern of conduct that permits any form of forced or 
   100  compulsory labor; the extent to which the failure of any economy to 
   101  establish and effectively enforce a

   167  46. Vietnam
   168  
   169      The governments of the remaining economies did not accept the Trade 
   170  Representative's request for consultations or were otherwise unable to 
   171  participate.
   172      Based on information obtained during the investigations, including 
   173  the confidential government-to-government consultations, the public 
   174  comments, testimony obtained at the public hearings, the confidential 
   175  advice of the appropriate advisory committees, and the Section 301 
   176  Committee, USTR prepared a comprehensive report, Acts, Policies, and 
   177  Practices of Various Economies Related to the Failure to Impose and 
   178  Effectively Enforce a Prohibition on the Importation of Goods Produced 
   179  with Forced Labor (the ``Report''), regarding the acts, policies, and 
   180  practices of each economy under investigation. For each investigation, 
   181  the Report supports determinations that the acts, policies, and 
   182  practices of each investigated economy related to the failure to impose 
   183  and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition are 
   184  unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus 
   185  actionable under Section 301 of the Trade Act. The Report is 
   186  incorporated by reference into this Notice, and is available on USTR's 
   187  website.
   188  
   189  II. The Acts, Policies, and Practices of the Investigated Economies 
   190  Related to the Failure To Impose and Effectively Enforce a Forced Labor 
   191  Import Prohibition
   192  
   193      Forced labor may be understood as work or service exacted from a 
   194  person under the menace of any penalty for its nonperformance and for 
   195  which the worker does not offer himself voluntarily. There is universal 
   196  international consensus that forced labor is a practice that should not 
   197  be tolerated. Numerous international instruments, such as the United 
   198  Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948); the International 
   199  Labour Organization (ILO) Abolition of Forced Labour Convention, 1957 
   200  (No. 105); the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights 
   201  (1976); and the ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at 
   202  Work and its Follow-up (1998), as amended in 2022, contain provisions 
   203  seeking to eliminate forced labor. Despite this clear and longstanding 
   204  consensus, the use of forced labor across the world continues to 
   205  persist and has even increased in recent years.
   206      The United States has long recognized that eliminating forced labor 
   207  is a moral and economic imperative and that trade is a critical means 
   208  to assist in that goal. For nearly 100 years, the United States has 
   209  prohibited the importation of goods produced with forced labor under 
   210  Section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1307). Commitments to 
   211  prohibit forced labor imports in the United States--Mexico--Canada 
   212  Agreement, as well as in recently signed Agreements on Reciprocal 
   213  Trade, reflect the increasing awareness of this issue and recognition 
   214  that the adverse effects of trade in forced labor goods must be 
   215  addressed.
   216      The existence of forced labor imports in markets across the globe 
   217  has nurtured an economic system that permits the use of forced labor or 
   218  forced labor inputs, penalizing firms and economies that do not. By 
   219  prohibiting forced labor domestically and effectively enforcing its 
   220  forced labor import prohibition, the United States aims to ensure that 
   221  neither domestically produced products nor imports can gain a 
   222  competitive advantage in the U.S. market through the use of forced 
   223  labor. This helps ensure that competition in the U.S. market is based 
   224  on legitimate factors, such as quality and innovation, rather than an 
   225  artificial cost advantage from the illicit use of forced labor.
   226      Economies that fail to impose and effectively enforce a forced 
   227  labor import prohibition fail to ensure that market competition in 
   228  their jurisdiction occurs on a level basis with respect to labor costs. 
   229  While the vast majority of economies prohibit forced labor 
   230  domestically, such measures, if effectively enforced, only discipline 
   231  domestic producers. However, as demonstrated in the Report, these 
   232  measures fail to discipline the influx of imported forced labor goods 
   233  or to prevent domestic producers from using forced labor inputs.
   234  
   235  III. Determinations on Acts, Policies, and Practices Under 
   236  Investigation
   237  
   238      Based on the information obtained during the investigations, as 
   239  reflected in the Report, and considering the advice of the appropriate 
   240  advisory committees and Section 301 Committee, the Trade Representative 
   241  has made the following determinations under sections 301(b) and 304(a) 
   242  of the Trade Act (19 U.S.C. 2411(b) and 2414(a)): the acts, policies, 
   243  and practices of each of the 60 economies covered in the investigations 
   244  are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and thus are 
   245  actionable under section 301(b) of the Trade Act.
   246  
   247  [[Page 34274]]
   248  
   249      In particular, the Trade Representative has determined:
   250       The following 54 economies have failed to impose and 
   251  effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced 
   252  with forced labor: Algeria; Angola; Argentina; Australia; the Bahamas; 
   253  Bahrain; Bangladesh; Brazil; Cambodia; Chile; China, People's Republic 
   254  of; Colombia; Costa Rica; Dominican Republic; Egypt; El Salvador; 
   255  Guatemala; Guyana; Honduras; Hong Kong, China; India; Iraq; Israel; 
   256  Japan; Jordan; Kazakhstan; Kuwait; Libya; Malaysia; Morocco; New 
   257  Zealand; Nicaragua; Nigeria; Norway; Oman; Peru; the Philippines; 
   258  Qatar; Russia; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; South Africa; South Korea; Sri 
   259  Lanka; Switzerland; Taiwan; Thailand; Trinidad and Tobago; 
   260  T[uuml]rkiye; United Arab Emirates; United Kingdom; Uruguay; Venezuela; 
   261  and Vietnam.
   262       The following six economies have failed to effectively 
   263  enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced 
   264  labor: Canada; Ecuador; the European Union; Indonesia; Mexico; and 
   265  Pakistan.
   266       Therefore, all of the investigated economies have failed 
   267  both to impose a forced labor import prohibition and to effectively 
   268  enforce such a prohibition.
   269       The failure of each of the investigated economies to 
   270  impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition is 
   271  unreasonable because it: (1) undermines the universal aim of 
   272  eliminating forced labor; (2) permits firms that avail themselves of 
   273  forced labor to produce goods at lower cost and thereby distort market 
   274  conditions for firms that do not use forced labor; (3) undermines the 
   275  profitability of firms that do not use forced labor; and (4) 
   276  contributes to the circumvention of existing forced labor import 
   277  prohibitions.
   278       The failure of each of the above-listed economies to 
   279  impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition 
   280  burdens or restricts U.S. commerce by subjecting U.S. producers to 
   281  unfair competition from forced labor goods both in export markets and 
   282  the U.S. market, and by displacing foreign goods produced without 
   283  forced labor or forced labor inputs into the United States and other 
   284  markets.
   285  
   286  IV. Proposed Actions To Be Taken in the Investigations
   287  
   288      Section 301(b) of the Trade Act provides that upon determining that 
   289  the acts, policies, and practices under investigation are actionable 
   290  and that action is appropriate, the Trade Representative shall take all 
   291  appropriate and feasible action authorized under section 301(c), 
   292  subject to the specific direction, if any, of the President regarding 
   293  such action, and all other appropriate and feasible action within the 
   294  power of the President, that the President may direct the Trade 
   295  Representative to take under section 301(b), to obtain the elimination 
   296  of that act, policy, or practice.
   297      Section 301(c) of the Trade Act authorizes the Trade Representative 
   298  to take certain actions for purposes of carrying out the provisions of 
   299  Section 301(b). Among others, Section 301(c)(1)(B) authorizes the Trade 
   300  Representative to ``impose duties or other import restrictions'' on the 
   301  goods of the foreign country subject to the investigation.
   302      Pursuant to Sections 301(b) and (c), the Trade Representative 
   303  proposes to determine that action is appropriate and that appropriate 
   304  action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices 
   305  would include the imposition of ad valorem duties on all products of 
   306  the 60 economies subject to investigations, except as provided in Annex 
   307  A to this Notice. The proposed exemptions in Annex A include all 
   308  articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs and raw 
   309  materials that if subject to the proposed additional tariffs could lead 
   310  to the unavailability of domestic supply. Annex A also includes 
   311  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to the 
   312  proposed additional tariffs and certain products that cannot be grown 
   313  or produced in sufficient quantities in the United States or obtained 
   314  from other sources. The proposed exemptions include informational 
   315  materials (e.g., books), donations, and accompanied baggage. Finally, 
   316  the proposed exemptions include articles for which additional tariffs 
   317  may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the investigated 
   318  acts, policies, and practices described above.
   319      For economies that impose a forced labor import prohibition--
   320  Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and Pakistan; 
   321  for economies that have undertaken commitments in their respective 
   322  Agreements on Reciprocal Trade regarding forced labor import 
   323  prohibitions--Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, 
   324  Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Taiwan; and economies that have 
   325  imposed a partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation 
   326  of certain forced labor goods--the United Kingdom; the Trade 
   327  Representative proposes additional duties of 10% for products of these 
   328  economies. For all other economies that have failed to impose and 
   329  effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition, the Trade 
   330  Representative proposes 12.5% as the rate of additional duties.
   331      The Trade Representative also proposes a textile mechanism that 
   332  would allow for a certain volume of apparel and textile imports to 
   333  enter the United States at a reduced Section 301 tariff rate. Under 
   334  such a textile mechanism, the volume of reduced-duty imports from 
   335  certain trading partners would be equivalent to the quantity of exports 
   336  of textiles (e.g., U.S. produced man-made and cotton fiber textile 
   337  inputs) from the United States to that trading partner. A certain 
   338  volume of apparel and textile imports would also be allowed to enter 
   339  the United States at the reduced Section 301 rate based on the volume 
   340  of U.S. cotton and cotton products a trading partner imports from the 
   341  United States during a certain period of time.
   342  
   343  V. Response to Significant Comments
   344  
   345      USTR responds below to significant issues raised in the public 
   346  comments and hearings in response to the March 17, 2026, Federal 
   347  Register notice.
   348  
   349  Response to Significant Comments Raising Legal Arguments Regarding 
   350  Findings of ``Unreasonableness''
   351  
   352      Multiple comments raised threshold arguments that the Trade 
   353  Representative should not find that the failure of an economy to impose 
   354  and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods 
   355  produced with forced labor is unreasonable where: (1) an economy has 
   356  domestic laws prohibiting forced labor; (2) where no international 
   357  standards exists which provide an affirmative obligation on economies 
   358  to impose a forced labor import prohibition; or (3) where an economy 
   359  has otherwise made commitments to the United States with respect to 
   360  imposing and/or enforcing a forced labor import prohibition. This 
   361  section takes each of these arguments in turn.
   362      With respect to the first argument, and as explained in the Report 
   363  and above, solely prohibiting forced labor domestically is unreasonable 
   364  because it fails to discipline the influx of forced labor goods or to 
   365  prevent domestic producers from using forced labor inputs. Thus, while 
   366  an economy may have taken steps to ensure that the condition of forced 
   367  labor is extinguished within its borders, the economy nevertheless 
   368  permits market conditions where imported forced labor goods have a 
   369  competitive advantage over U.S. goods imported into their economy.
   370      In response to the second argument, USTR notes the Section 301 
   371  statute,
   372  
   373  [[Page 34275]]
   374  
   375  which governs these investigations, does not require the existence of 
   376  international standards discipling specific conduct as a prerequisite 
   377  to a finding of an unreasonable act, policy, or practice under Section 
   378  301(b) of the Trade Act. As explained in the Report, the definition of 
   379  unreasonable acts, policies, and practices in Section 301(d) 
   380  contemplates circumstances where, as here, acts, policies, and 
   381  practices of a foreign country may not be inconsistent with or violate 
   382  the international legal rights of the United States, but are 
   383  nevertheless unfair. Thus, the statutory structure of Section 301 
   384  contemplates that the Trade Representative may find unreasonable 
   385  conduct on the part of a trading partner even in the absence of 
   386  international standards or obligations.
   387      Third, some comments argued that where an economy has made 
   388  commitments to the United States regarding forced labor import 
   389  prohibitions, including through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, the 
   390  Trade Representative is without basis to find that same economy's 
   391  failure to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
   392  prohibition is unreasonable. USTR applauds Argentina, Bangladesh, 
   393  Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and 
   394  Taiwan, which have undertaken commitments regarding a forced labor 
   395  import prohibition. However, commitments to take action in the future 
   396  is distinct from forbidding legally the importation of forced labor 
   397  goods, and effectively enforcing such prohibition. Until such time as 
   398  the commitment is implemented, U.S. products will continue to compete 
   399  against forced labor products that have a competitive advantage in

Aha! Statement 2 "USTR received over 450 written comments and heard nearly 60 witnesses." That's exactly June proposal's description of comments to March 17 initiation, not the July action's comments. The adopted notice says over 1,600 comments and >100 witnesses. Statement likely "about forced-labor action" but could be true of proposal? It says "After June proposal..."? No statement 2 alone: "USTR received over 450 written comments on the proposed action and heard nearly 60 witnesses." This conflates June proposal's prior comment stats (450 / 60) with proposed action. The adopted notice says 1,600 / 100. So incorrect. Q14 asks where documents differ. Good.

Need read remainder June proposal for proposed rates and Annex A, particularly dates and exemptions. Also Q11 discrepancies. Let's read 400-988.

   412      A number of comments responded on potential responsive action by

   427  VI. Request for Public Comments
   428  
   429      In accordance with section 304(b) of the Trade Act (19 U.S.C. 
   430  2414(b)), USTR invites comments from interested persons with respect to 
   431  the proposed actions to be taken in the investigations. To be assured 
   432  of consideration, you must submit written comments on the proposed 
   433  actions by July 6, 2026, in accordance with the instructions in section 
   434  VIII below.

   436  regarding:
   437       The specific products to be subject to increased duties, 
   438  including whether products should be retained or removed from the scope 
   439  of the action, or whether products currently listed in Annex A should 
   440  be added to the scope of the action;
   441       Whether products listed in Annex A are appropriately 
   442  excluded;
   443       The level of the increase, if any, in the rate of duty;

   445  economy where the economy has made a commitment to the United States to 
   446  impose and enforce a forced labor import prohibition; has imposed a 
   447  forced labor import prohibition; or has imposed a partial regime with 
   448  the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods.
   449       Features of a textile mechanism, including the U.S. and 
   450  foreign products to be covered, the relative market opportunities for 
   451  each side, and the tariff rate (if any) to be applied to products 
   452  subject to that mechanism, as well as whether a similar mechanism 
   453  should apply to any other product or sector.
   454      In considering whether certain articles should be subject to 
   455  additional duties under Section 301, USTR will consider the needs of 
   456  the U.S. economy. In commenting on the inclusion or removal of 
   457  particular tariff subheadings subject to the proposed action, USTR 
   458  requests that comments address specifically whether the products under 
   459  the tariff subheading are necessary raw materials that if subject to 
   460  the proposed additional tariffs could lead to the unavailability of 
   461  domestic supply; whether additional tariffs would cause serious 
   462  dislocations in the supply of the products and could cause economy-wide 
   463  disruptions, or other similar factors; and whether imposing additional 
   464  tariffs on products under the tariff subheading would be practicable or 
   465  effective in obtaining the elimination of the investigated acts, 
   466  policies, and practices.
   467      Additional instructions on how to submit written comments are 
   468  provided in section VIII below.

   470  VII. Hearing Participation
   471  
   472      The Section 301 Committee will convene public hearings beginning on 
   473  July 7, 2026, in the main hearing room of the U.S. International Trade 
   474  Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, beginning at 10:00 
   475  a.m. The hearings may continue, as appropriate. To testify at the 
   476  hearings, you must submit a request to appear using the electronic 
   477  portal at https://comments.ustr.gov/s/, following the instructions in 
   478  Part VIII below.
   479      Requests to appear must include a summary of testimony, and may be 
   480  accompanied by a pre-hearing submission. USTR will announce details of 
   481  the hearing at a later time. All submissions must be in English. To be 
   482  assured of consideration, USTR must receive your request to appear and 
   483  summary of the testimony by June 22, 2026.
   484  
   485  VIII. Procedures for Written Comments
   486  
   487      You must submit requests to appear at the hearings or written 
   488  comments using the appropriate docket on the portal at https://comments.ustr.gov/s/. All submissions must be in English.
   489      Interested persons wishing to provide testimony at the hearings 
   490  must submit a notification of intent and summary of testimony using the 
   491  docket entitled ``Request to Appear at the Hearing on Proposed Action 
   492  in the Section 301 Investigations of Acts, Policies, and Practices of 
   493  Various Economies Related to the Failure to Impose and Effectively 
   494  Enforce a Prohibition on the Importation of Goods Produced with Forced 
   495  Labor,'' docket number USTR-2026-0266.
   496      To submit written comments, including rebuttal comments, use the 
   497  docket on the portal entitled ``Request for Comments Concerning 
   498  Proposed Action in Section 301 Investigations of Various Economies 
   499  Related to the Failure to Impose and Effectively
   500  
   501  [[Page 34276]]
   502  
   503  Enforce a Prohibition on the Importation of Goods Produced with Forced 
   504  Labor Rights'', docket number USTR-2026-0265.
   505      You do not need to establish an account to submit comments. The 
   506  first screen of each docket allows you to enter identification and 
   507  contact information. Third party organizations such as law firms, trade 
   508  associations, or customs brokers, should identify the full legal name 
   509  of the organization they represent, and identify the primary point of 
   510  contact for the submission. Information fields are optional; however, 
   511  your comment or request may not be considered if insufficient 
   512  information is provided.
   513      Fields with a gray Business Confidential Information (BCI) notation 
   514  are for BCI information which will not be made publicly available. 
   515  Fields with a green (Public) notation will be viewable by the public.
   516      After entering the identification and contact information, you can 
   517  complete the remainder of the comment, or any portion of it by clicking 
   518  ``Next.'' You may upload documents at the end of the form and indicate 
   519  whether USTR should treat the documents as business confidential or 
   520  public information.
   521      Any page containing BCI must be clearly marked `BUSINESS 
   522  CONFIDENTIAL' on the top of that page and the submission should clearly 
   523  indicate, via brackets, highlighting, or other means, the specific 
   524  information that is BCI. If you request business confidential 
   525  treatment, you must certify in writing that disclosure of the 
   526  information would endanger trade secrets or profitability, and that the 
   527  information would not customarily be released to the public.
   528      Parties uploading attachments containing BCI also must submit a 
   529  public version of their comments. If these procedures are not 
   530  sufficient to protect BCI or otherwise protect business interests, 
   531  please contact the USTR Section 301 support line at (202) 395-5725 to 
   532  discuss whether alternative arrangements are possible.

   534  inspection, except for properly designated BCI. You can view

content.text:
June proposal excludes USMCA-compliant Canada/Mexico, section 232 goods. Adopted notice has Canada USMCA exemption (heading 9903.05.93) and Mexico (9903.05.94) but only for specific country headings, effectively same. Section 232 exemption remains. Q9(c) Mexico USMCA claim => section 301 0; no claim => 12.5% of 50k = 6,250. Need check Mexico rate is 10%, not 12.5! Wait Mexico is in 10% flat list due to failed enforcement. Yes 10%. Q9(c) no USMCA claim => 10% = 5,000. Good.

Q6 rates: Canada irrelevant.

Need Q7. Non-ad valorem rule at note 52(k). For France (EU) specific duty 3 cents/kg, customs value $12k, 2,000kg. Duty payable under column 1 = $0.03*2000 = $60. Ad valorem equivalent = 60/12000 = 0.5%. Since EU net-of-MFN total 10%, section 301 = 9.5%? Wait additional duty rate is difference between 10 and MFN AVE 0.5 = 9.5%. But what is base for applying percentage? Section 301 duty is 9.5% of customs value = $1,140. Total MFN $60 + 301 $1,140 = $1,200 = 10%. Good.
(b) compound 4% + 25c/kg, 4,000kg, value 20k. MFN duty = 4%*20,000 = 800 + 0.25*4,000=1,000 => 1,800; AVE=9%. Italy EU: section 301 = 1% of value = 200 (so total 10%). Japan: net 12.5, MFN 9 <12.5, section 301 = 3.5% = 700. Brazil: flat 12.5%=2,500. Need perhaps for Brazil section 301 applies to customs value, not MFN. yes.
(c) MFN duty $2,200 on $20,000 = 11%. Taiwan net 10: MFN >=10 => section 301 = 0. Switzerland net 12.5: MFN 11 <12.5 => 1.5% = $300.
(d) Rule note 52(k) at 91 FR 47394, and result for equivalent rate at or above cap stated at 91 FR 47394: where applicable column 1 duty rate is >= 10/12.5, section 301 zero (for Taiwan/EU etc.). Need precise.

Q2(a) 50% duty. But wait if wine is on Annex II and not excluded. Entry Aug 20/21 before effective Aug 22 -> no 338. Entry Aug 22 12:01 -> duty applies. $40k * 50% = 20k. Need cite clause (1) and suspension clause (1). Good.
Q2(c) broker deposited duty on entry 1: refund under Proclamation 11056 clause (4), plus perhaps because not owed. Need say "refund shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP standard procedures for such refunds." There may also be CBP implementation notice (not found). Search for "Aug. 22" / "11056" CBP. But likely enough.

Q3(b) FTZ. Need examine original proclamation clause 4: "Any product subject to duties imposed in this proclamation, except those eligible for domestic status, that ... is admitted into a FTZ on or after effective date must be admitted as privileged foreign status, and will be subject upon entry for consumption to any ad valorem rate of duty related to classification." Here admitted Sept 25, after effective date, so privileged foreign status. Upon withdrawal Oct 6, the product is subject to import ban? Since exclusion applies to "goods imported on or after September 29." Is FTZ admission an importation? Under 19 CFR 146, admission to FTZ is not entry for consumption and goods are not "imported" until entry. But clause 2 says "Products that will be subject to the import ban ... that were imported, but not yet entered for consumption ... prior to September 29 remain subject to 50%." If FTZ admission is not importation, then no. However "imported" in trade law can mean brought into U.S. customs territory; FTZ is outside customs territory. So FTZ goods admitted Sept 25 likely not "imported" before Sept 29. The ban applies to importation on/after Sept 29, so entry for consumption Oct 6 is prohibited. But perhaps privileged foreign status allows it to be entered? No, an import prohibition would bar entry. Need see if HTSUS note/Annex includes a FTZ carveout. Exclusion proclamation has no FTZ clause. Hmm.

Could there be a CBP rule implementing exclusions stating foreign trade zone admissions? Search Federal Register for section 338 Canada CBP notices.

content.text:
No CBP notices. Fine.

Q4: Products X/Y/Z subject to 25% 232. On Sept 10, original 338 applies Aug 22 but clause (2) excludes 232 goods => no 338 for all. On Oct 1:
- X alcohol: scope mod 18838 effective Sept 15 says duties as modified apply in addition to 232. Was X in Annex I Part A? Scenario says X is listed in Annex II original, none other list. Wait Q4 says "Product X is listed in Annex II of alcoholic-beverages duty proclamation... None of them is on any other list." Q5 later has Annex I parts. For Q4, X only Annex II, not modified. Original clause 2 excluded 232. Does 18838's clause 1 make all original Annex II products apply in addition to 232, or only products in Annex I Part A? Text: "certain products ... as set forth in Annex I, Part A ... shall be subject ... In addition, certain products ... Part B ... shall no longer be subject... The duties imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11046, as modified in this proclamation, shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232..." Does this override original clause 2 for all products or only Annex I Part A? "as modified" means scope modified by Parts A/B, and for those duties apply in addition to 232. If X is not on any Annex I part (assumed no other list), maybe original exclusion still applies, so no 338 even Oct 1. But Q4 likely tests that after scope modifications, 338 stacks on 232 only for products in scope modification. Need parse carefully.

Q4 explicitly: "Product X is listed in Annex II of the alcoholic-beverages duty proclamation, product Y in Annex II of the dairy duty proclamation, and product Z in Annex II of the motor-vehicles duty proclamation. None of them is on any other list." So X not in Annex I A/B of alcohol scope mod. Y no dairy scope. Z no Sept/Oct Part A/B. None on exclusion lists. Each subject to 232. On Sept 10: original clause 2 excludes all. On Oct 1: Have scope modifications changed the 232 exclusion for products not on A/B? The new sentence says "The duties imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11048, as modified in this proclamation, shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232." Could be a general override: the duties "as modified" (i.e., the whole amended action) apply in addition. But for X not changed, the duty still imposed by Proclamation 11046, as modified? The phrase could apply to all remaining covered products. Q4 likely expects 338 to apply to all three from Sept 15 because scope mods override 232 exclusion generally. But the clause appears in both alcohol and motor vehicle scope mods; dairy no scope mod, so Y still no 338. Q4 tests this: X and Z get 338 after Sept 15; Y remains exempt. Need decide.

Let's parse original clause (2): "Except as otherwise provided in this proclamation and in Annex I, the duties imposed in this proclamation are in addition to any other duties... The duties imposed in this proclamation shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232..." Scope mod clause (1): "Except as otherwise provided in this proclamation, certain products ... Annex I, Part A ... shall be subject to [50%]. In addition, certain products ... Part B ... shall no longer be subject... The duties imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11046, as modified in this proclamation, shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232." This seems to expressly supersede the 232 carve-out for all duties imposed pursuant to 11046 as modified, not just Part A. If so X and Z stack from Sept 15. Why say "as modified"? Because scope modifications redefine product list. "The duties imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11046, as modified in this proclamation" = all remaining duties under 11046. I think Q4 expects this. Y (dairy) has no equivalent modification, so original 232 exclusion remains; no 338. Q4 likely tests asymmetry: alcohol and motor vehicles scope mods stack with 232; dairy still doesn't. On Oct 1 X 50k, Z 50k, Y 0. On Sept 10 all 0. Need state exact text at 58332 and 58340, and original clause 2 at 46640/46654/46664. Good.

Q5: Need understand Annex I Part A/B semantics for Sept and Oct proclamations:
- Sept 18839: Part A = products newly subject? Text says "certain products ... Part A ... shall be subject to 50%." Part B = "shall no longer be subject." Given P is in Part A and not original => newly added. Q in original and Part B => removed.So Part A adds, Part B removes.
- Oct 22292: Part A = "shall no longer be subject"; Part B = "shall be subject." So reversed! Thus R original + Oct Part A => removed Oct 30. S Part B only => added Oct 30.
Effective Sept 15 00:01 and Oct 30 00:01.
Q5(a) times:
P: 3pm Sept 14 no; 12:01am Sept 15 yes; 4pm Oct 29 yes; 12:01am Oct 30? P not in Oct lists, so remains yes; Nov 3 yes.
Q: 3pm Sept 14 yes (original); 12:01am Sept 15 no (Part B removal); 4pm Oct 29 no; 12:01am Oct 30 no (not in Oct); Nov 3 no.
R: 3pm Sept 14 yes; 12:01am Sept 15 yes (not in Sept Part B); 4pm Oct 29 yes; 12:01am Oct 30 no (Oct Part A removal); Nov 3 no.
S: 3pm Sept 14 no; 12:01am Sept 15 no; 4pm Oct 29 no; 12:01am Oct 30 yes (Oct Part B); Nov 3 yes.
Need carefully assess "12:01 a.m. on Sept 15" applies to entries on or after 12:01; yes.
Q5(b): Oct proclamation signed Oct 23, filed with OFR Oct 29 (from FR Doc filed line "Filed 10-29-26; 11:15 am"), published Oct 30, applies 12:01am Oct 30. Do scope proclamations reach entries before they apply? No, effective only entries on/after. Do they provide refunds? No refund provision. Text silent. If duties paid before, no refund mechanism. Need say not retroactive; no refund clause. But could entries made before effective date that are still subject? No.
Q5(c): Waiting period: 30 days after signing. P signed? September scope proclamation signed Sept 8, applies Sept 15 = 7 days after signing. But P was new, so section 338 says not earlier than 30 days after proclamation finding. How fits? Maybe the original July 20 proclamation contained the finding; September scope proclamation only modifies scope, not new finding, so 30-dayclock ran from July 20 to Aug 19; P added Sept 15 after that. Similarly S added Oct 30 after original finding. Scope proclamations explain? They say section 338 authorizes duties not to take effect earlier than 30 days after President's proclamation finding. They don't expressly explain why additions can take effect quickly; likely because finding was in original proclamation and 30 days elapsed. Q asks "do the scope proclamations explain how that fits the waiting period?" They recite the 30-day limit but do not explain. Need note that they rely on original finding; P/S became dutiable 7 days after Sept signing (P: Sept 8 to Sept 15) and 7 days after Oct signing (S: Oct 23 to Oct 30), less than 30 days, but more than 30 days after July 20 original finding (57 days and 102 days). Documents don't expressly reconcile. This is a potential discrepancy or gap. But maybe Q11 discrepancy: scope proclamations say 30 days after "President's proclamation finding," and each scope proclamation itself includes findings? It says "Section 338 authorizes... not to take effect earlier than 30 days after the President's proclamation finding that a foreign country is imposing..." Then clause effective 7 days. Could be discrepancy within same document! Q11 wants statements about what action provides vs operative text. The recital says 30-day wait, operative imposes in 7 days. But original finding satisfies. Hmm.

Need Q1 details: every presidential document in section 338 series. Need date/time each operative change applies and what event measured against. Let's map:
- 11046 alcohol: signed 7/20, published 7/23, imposes 50% on Annex II; operative effective 12:01am ET Aug 19, measured against entry for consumption or withdrawal from warehouse for consumption. Later suspension changes effective date to Aug 22. But Q1 says "date and time from which its operative change applies. Say which kind of event that date and time is measured against in each document." For each doc as originally issued? We can say as issued Aug 19; as amended Aug 22; measured against entry/withdrawal. Q1 maybe wants current operative date. Need list both perhaps.
- 11047 dairy same.
- 11048 motor vehicles same.
- 11056 suspension: effective date changed to Aug 22, measured against entry/withdrawal. Signed Aug 18, published Aug 24.No separate effective date; clause (1) says "shall be 12:01am Aug 22." Does it apply retroactively? It was signed Aug 18 before original Aug 19, so yes. Time measured against entry/withdrawal per amended annex? The suspension clause itself just changes effective date. 
- 11061 alcohol exclusion: effective Sept 29 12:01am, measured against goods "imported on or after" (not entry). Important distinction.
- 11062 dairy exclusion: same Sept 29 "imported on or after."
- 11063 motor vehicle exclusion: same Sept 29 "imported on or after."
- 11064 alcohol scope mod: effective Sept 15 12:01am, measured against entry/withdrawal.
- 11065 motor vehicle scope mod: effective Sept 15 12:01am, measured against entry/withdrawal.
- 11076 further MV scope: effective Oct 30 12:01am, measured against entry/withdrawal.
No dairy scope modification. Total 10.

Product group changes:
Alcohol: 11046 imposes on Annex II; 11056 delays; 11064 adds Part A, removes Part B; 11061 bans Annex products from importation (effective Sept 29), converting them from duty to prohibition; clause 3 says others unaffected.
Dairy: 11047 imposes Annex II; 11056 delays; 11062 bans Annex products; no dairy scope modification published (even though 11062 clause 3 refers to one).
Motor vehicles: 11048 imposes Annex II; 11056 delays; 11065 adds Part A, removes Part B; 11063 bans Annex products from Sept 29; 11076 removes Part A, adds Part B effective Oct 30. Note chronology: exclusion of certain MV products Sept 29, then Oct 30 scope changes might remove duty on products already banned? Need mention. But Q1 asks which docs changed which products subject to duty. 11076 changes duty scope but doesn't affect import ban? It says duties only, no mention ban. Could create overlap? We'll describe.

Now Q6 exact rates. Need determine 10 economies:
1 Switzerland: 12.5 net MFN. MFN 4%, section 301 8.5%, total MFN $4,000 + 301 $8,500 = $12,500.
2 Norway: 12.5 flat. 301 $12,500; total $16,500.
3 UK: 10 flat. $10,000; total $14,000.
4 Germany (EU): 10 net. 4% MFN => 6% = $6,000; total $10,000.
5 Taiwan: 10 net. 4% => 6% = $6,000; total $10,000.
6 Türkiye: 12.5 flat. $12,500; total $16,500.
7 Japan: 12.5 net. 4% => 8.5% = $8,500; total $12,500.
8 Liechtenstein: not investigated! Section 301 no duty. $0; total $4,000. Important.
9 Hong Kong: 12.5 flat. $12,500; total $16,500.
10 India: 10 flat. $10,000; total $14,000.
Need check if exemptions apply to these products. Scenario just "a product" MFN 4; assume not exempt? It doesn't state annex status. We may need caveat that duty assumes product not exempt under Annex I/II; if on list, zero. Q6 likely expects rates only.

(b):
- Germany MFN 12% => EU net 10, MFN >=10 => 301 $0.
- Japan MFN 12% => net 12.5, 301 = 0.5% of 100k = $500.
- Taiwan MFN exactly 10% => 301 $0.
- South Korea MFN exactly 10% => 12.5 net, 301 2.5% = $2,500.
- Switzerland MFN free => 12.5% = $12,500.
(c) Compare June proposal vs adopted:
June proposed 10% for Canada, Ecuador, EU, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan (imposed bans), ART economies Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, Taiwan, and UK partial regime. All others 12.5%. No net-of-MFN in June; flat rates. Adopted:
- Switzerland: June 12.5 flat, adopted 12.5 net => treatment differs (rate net of MFN).
- Norway: June 12.5, adopted 12.5 flat => same.
- UK: June 10, adopted 10 => same.
- Germany/EU: June 10 flat, adopted 10net => differs.
- Taiwan: June 10 flat (ART), adopted 10 net => differs.
- Türkiye: 12.5 both => same.
- Japan: June 12.5 flat, adopted 12.5 net => differs.
- Liechtenstein: not investigated, no action both.
- Hong Kong: 12.5 both.
- India: June 12.5 (not in 10 list; no ART), adopted 10 flat because adopted forced-labor ban after June => rate changed; reason stated India adopted ban after June 5.
Any other economy whose rate itself changed among ten? Only India. Maybe Taiwan remains 10 but net; EU net; Japan/Switzerland net. Good.
Need mention Canada? Not asked.
Q6(c) "For which of ten economies in (a) does adopted treatment differ from what was proposed in June 2026, and how? For any economy whose rate itself changed, give reason documents state." Answer: India rate changed 12.5 to 10 because adopted forced-labor import prohibition after June 5; others same nominal but net-of-MFN for EU/Taiwan/Japan/Switzerland. Norway/UK/Türkiye/Hong Kong unchanged; Liechtenstein not subject.

Q7 done.

Q8 Dominican Republic. Adopted rate 12.5% flat. Effective July 24 12:01am, except goods loaded onto vessel at port of loading and in transit on final mode of transit before 12:01am July 24, and entered/withdrawn before 12:01am July 28, not subject. This is transit exception. Need apply to seven:
1 loaded July 22, entered July 29: loaded before July 24, but entered after July 28 00:01 => exception not available; duty 12.5% of 80k = 10k.
2 same sailing entered July 27 3pm: loaded before July 24, entered before July 28 => exempt, 0.
3 entered July 28 12:01am: exception requires before 12:01am July 28. At exactly 12:01 not before => duty 10k.
4 loaded July 24 6am (after cutoff), entered July 27: exception requires loaded before 12:01am July 24, fails; duty 10k even though entered before 28.
5 entered July 23: before effective date July 24 => 0.
6 arrived June, bonded warehouse, withdrawn July 26: The exception says goods loaded onto a vessel at port of loading and in transit on final mode before July 24 and entered/withdrawn before July 28. But these goods arrived June, were in bonded warehouse, not "in transit on final mode" before July 24? They are in warehouse. Duty applies to withdrawals on/after July 24; 12.5% =10k. Unless "entered for consumption or withdrawn ... before July 28" and in transit before July 24, but not in transit. So duty.
7 air freight loaded July 23 9pm, entered July 25: exception says "loaded onto a vessel at the port of loading and in transit on the final mode of transit" — air freight is not vessel. So exception unavailable; duty 10k. Important.
(b) Rule where? DATES line at 91 FR 47318, and maybe U.S. note 52? Cite 91 FR 47318. Also Q8(b) "exactly where rule for goods in transit is stated" – DATES line. Could also Notice section? Search "loaded onto a vessel".

(c) signed July 23, effective July 24 12:01am, published July 28. Memorandum signed July 23, published July 28; notice same.
(d) Patented pharmaceutical article heading 9903.04.62, product Dominican Republic, entered July 30 and Aug 3. Annex I note 2.B effective July 31, 2026 modifies 9903.05.90 to include "patented pharmaceutical articles" and note 52(f)(8) "patented pharmaceutical articles provided for in headings 9903.04.60-9903.04.66." So from July 31, exempt. July 30: not yet exempt; 12.5% of 80k = 10k. Aug 3: exempt, 0. Need check heading 9903.04.62 is within range yes. This is likely test of delayed effective date of pharma exemption. Good.

Q9:
(a) Thailand machine under 9802.00.80, assembled article value 100k incl US components 35k. Note 52(a): additional duties apply to value of article assembled abroad less cost/value of US products = 100k - 35k = 65k. Thailand rate 12.5% = 8,125. MFN irrelevant? 9802 program means duty on value of foreign components etc. The section 301 duty base 65k. Need cite 91 FR 47352.
(b) US machine returned from Israel after repairs cost 6k, entered 9802.00.50. Note 52(a): for subheading 9802.00.50, additional duties apply to value of repairs/alterations/processing. Treat repairs as product of Israel. Israel rate? Israel is 12.5 flat (not 10; it's a developed economy but not UK/ART). So 6,000 * 12.5% = $750. Need check if Israel exempt? It's investigated and 12.5. Yes.
(c) Mexico 5% MFN value 50k: (i) USMCA free => section 301 0 under heading 9903.05.94 (Mexico products entered free of duty under USMCA). (ii) no claim => 10% flat = 5,000. MFN duty 5% = 2,500 but question asks section 301. Note total if needed? It asks "What section 301 duty" only. Could mention MFN separately.
(d) Japanese passenger car under section 232 heading 9903.94.01, value 40k. Section 301 note 52(f)(2) exempts passenger vehicles provided for in 9903.94.01 from section 301. So $0. Need confirm no 12.5 net because exempt. 
(e) Brazil product 100k subject to 232 under chapter 99 heading not mentioned in section 301 note. Is it exempt? Note 52(f) exempts only enumerated 232 headings, not all 232 goods? Wait June proposal said all articles subject to section 232, but adopted note 52(f) lists specific headings. Text in notice says "all articles and parts of articles subject to tariffs under Section 232" proposed, but adopted text may narrow? Let's inspect note 52(f) exact: "As provided in heading 9903.05.90, the additional duties ... shall not apply to: (1) articles of aluminum, of steel or of copper, nor to derivative aluminum or steel articles provided for in headings 9903.82.02 and 9903.82.04-9903.82.26; (2)...". So only listed 232 categories. If Brazil's 232 heading not mentioned, then not exempt, 12.5% = 12,500. Q9(e) likely tests that adopted text does NOT exempt all section 232 goods, contrary to proposal/general statement. Need say section 301 applies because exemption is limited to enumerated headings and this one is not mentioned. Also note 52(a) says all products subject to additional duties also subject to any additional duty in subchapter IV? "shall also be subject to any additional duty provided for in this subchapter or subchapter IV" but 232 in subchapter III? Anyway. 
(f) June proposal vs adopted on 232 and informational materials/donations. June Annex A note lines 567-573: proposed action does not cover informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage; all articles/parts subject to section 232; USMCA-compliant Canada/Mexico; CAFTA-DR textiles. Adopted notice: Did it retain informational materials and donations? Need search. Grep didn't find "informational materials" after line 170; only proposal description in preamble. Maybe adopted Annex I note 52 doesn't mention them at all. Hmm note 52(c) particular articles, (f) 232, (g)/(h) USMCA, etc. No informational materials/donations/accompanied baggage except note 52(a) "other than products for personal use included in accompanied baggage." So adopted text may only exempt accompanied baggage, not informational materials/donations. The summary/preamble line 170 says proposals included these, but no adopted exemption. Q9(f) asks "What did June 2026 proposal say ... and about informational materials and donations? What does adopted text say on each?" So answer: proposal expressly exempted informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage, and all section 232 articles/parts. Adopted text: 232 exemption narrowed to enumerated headings in note 52(f); informational materials and donations are not mentioned in operative text (only accompanied baggage in note 52(a)); so not exempt (unless within Annex). Need verify no HTSUS general note exemption elsewhere. Search "books", "donations".
