content.text:
Important discrepancy Q11: Notice preamble at 91 FR 47318 says June proposal included exemptions for informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage, all section 232. That's accurate about proposal. But adopted notice text at 47334 says "many inputs, including auto parts already subject to Section 232 tariffs, are exempt from additional tariffs pursuant to this action" — only many, not all. Could be okay if those in list. But Q9(f) asks what adopted text says on each; likely no exemption for informational materials/donations; 232 only enumerated. Need be clear.

Q14 statement 5 "Every economy whose rate is net of the MFN rate also has its own negotiated list of exempt products." EU, Taiwan, Switzerland have Parts C/K/D; Japan/Korea not. Could be "own negotiated list" in Annex I? All economies have Part A common plus country-specific. Japan/Korea just common. So incorrect.

Q14 statement 8: FTZ rule. The notice says "Any product ... subject to additional duty ... admitted into a U.S. foreign trade zone, except any product eligible for admission under domestic status, only may be admitted as privileged foreign status, effective as of the date that the additional duty is imposed." Statement says "Goods admitted to a foreign trade zone once the duties apply must be admitted in privileged foreign status, unless they are eligible for domestic status." Correct. But maybe wording "once the duties apply" okay. Need distinguish Q3(b) section 338 FTZ clause similar but not exactly: section 338 clause says "Any product subject to duties ... except those eligible for domestic status ... admitted ... on or after effective date must be admitted as privileged foreign status, and will be subject upon entry for consumption to any ad valorem rate of duty..." So yes.

Q14 statement 1: Memorandum says "establishing these TRQs is not feasible at this time, but ... will be feasible by September 1, 2026" — not a deadline to set up. It directs as soon as feasible; no Sept 1 deadline. So incorrect (or partly: memo mentions Sept 1 feasibility). 
Statement 2: June proposal says over 450 comments and nearly 60 witnesses regarding March initiation; adopted notice says >1,600 comments and >100 witnesses on proposed action. If statement refers to "proposed action" after June, incorrect. It might be testing conflation. 
Statement 3: "seven economies were moved from 12.5 percent to 10 percent because each adopted a forced-labor import ban." The seven are Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago (adopted bans) + Jordan (ART commitment). So partly correct; six adopted bans, Jordan commitment. Also were all 12.5 in June? Yes likely. Need verify June proposed 12.5 for these. June list: 10% for Canada, Ecuador, EU, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan; ART Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, Taiwan; UK. So Cambodia/Guatemala were already 10% in June! Wait! June proposal included Cambodia and Guatemala in ART 10% list. So they were not moved from 12.5. Let's re-read. June list lines 319-327: economies that impose ban: Canada, Ecuador, EU, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan; ART: Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, Taiwan; UK partial. Thus Cambodia and Guatemala were already proposed 10%, not 12.5. Adopted additional economies after June: Cambodia (already 10), Guatemala (already 10), Honduras (12.5 -> 10), India (12.5 -> 10), Sri Lanka (12.5 -> 10), Trinidad and Tobago (12.5 -> 10), Jordan (12.5 ->10). Wait adopted notice says additional economies imposed bans: Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago; but Cambodia/Guatemala already in ART at 10. So only Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad, Jordan moved from 12.5 to 10? Maybe Cambodia and Guatemala were already 10 but their status changed from ART commitment to adopted ban; not rate change. Statement says seven economies moved from 12.5 to 10 because each adopted ban—incorrect in multiple ways: only four adopted bans moved from 12.5 (Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad), plus Jordan moved due ART, and Cambodia/Guatemala already 10. Unless June had 12.5 for all except six/UK? Wait June summary lines 45-51 says 10% for economies that impose ban, ART, partial regime; then lines 319-327 explicitly lists. Yes Cambodia/Guatemala in ART 10. So statement 3 false/partly. Need explain.

But perhaps Q14 statement 3 intentionally says "seven economies were moved from 12.5 percent to 10 percent because each of them adopted a forced-labor import ban." The adopted notice says additional economies after June: Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago imposed bans; Jordan ART. It may imply all seven moved, but only some. This could be a discrepancy between notice's preamble and rate lists: at 91 FR 47319 it says "additional economies have imposed ... Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago; or ... Jordan." It doesn't say rates changed. Statement inaccurate. Need mention.

Q14 statement 4: beef/avocados. Text says comments requested removal; USTR "determined not to remove these products from the list of exempted products." So incorrect. 
Statement 6: "471 more products than proposed, including all sugar and sugar-containing products." Text says additional 471 products, "certain sugar and sugar-containing products." So partly; not all.
Statement 7: "USTR stated that no product will bear more than 12.5 percent duty in total." Need search "maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent" at 47334. That says "particularly with maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent" in context of economy-wide disruptions. But that's maximum section 301 tariff, not total duty. No statement "no product total >12.5". Could be inference. The documents say for net economies sum of MFN + 301 = 10 or 12.5; for flat-rate economies 301 is 12.5 on top of MFN, so total can exceed 12.5. Statement incorrect. Need cite memo section 1(a)(ii)-(iii) 91 FR 47720 and notice lines 434-469.
Statement 10: "Of products on proposal's Annex A, the only ones USTR cut back were certain chemicals." Text says exactly "exempt all products proposed ... except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products." Then determined not to remove other products. So correct. But is "cut back" ambiguous—limited exemption to pharma applications. Correct.

Q11: Need find discrepancies between documents/statements and operative text in section 301 and section 338 actions. We need be thorough, list as many as possible. Need inspect all documents and compare. This is likely designed with planted inconsistencies. We need identify carefully. Let's parse each action.

Section 301 action:
- June proposal (2026-11296)
- Memorandum (2026-15274)
- Notice (2026-15181)
Potential discrepancies:
1. Memorandum says "The Trade Representative proposed tariffs of 10 percent ad valorem on goods of economies that: impose a forced labor import prohibition but do not yet effectively enforce it (Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and Pakistan)..." June proposal says same. Fine.
2. Memorandum says "USTR received over 1,600 written comments and testimony from over 100 witnesses at the hearings." Notice says same. Fine.
3. Memorandum says "TRQs ... establishing these TRQs is not feasible at this time, but ... feasible by September 1, 2026." Notice says "will establish ... in separate notice" and no deadline. Not necessarily discrepancy; memo recital vs operative.
4. Memorandum Section 1(a)(i) 10% list includes Canada, etc. Notice summary line 436-439 includes same 17, but omits Canada? Let's count: notice line 436-439: Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago, and UK. Same 17. Good.
5. Notice summary says 10% rate for "an economy that imposes a forced labor import prohibition, has committed ... ART, or has imposed a partial regime..." But the operative list includes countries that merely committed in ART; fine.
6. Notice line 147-154 says six economies "failed to effectively enforce" but then "All ... have failed to impose ... and effectively enforce..." consistent.
7. Notice preamble line 170 says June proposals included exemptions for informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage, all 232 articles. June proposal Annex A indeed says so. Adopted text does not include informational materials/donations; only accompanied baggage, enumerated 232. Is that a discrepancy between notice's description of proposal and adopted text? The statement is about proposal, not adopted, so not inaccurate. But Q11 asks "places where a statement in one document about what the action provides, or about what another document of same action says or does, differs from operative text." A statement in adopted notice about proposal doesn't purport to describe adopted action. But Q9(f) asks adopted text. Maybe Q11 can list notice's general statement at 47334 "auto parts already subject to Section 232 tariffs are exempt" vs operative note 52(f) enumerates only certain auto parts headings, but it says "many inputs, including auto parts" not all. No discrepancy.
8. Notice says "The Trade Representative has determined to exempt the products listed in Annexes I and II ... each of these products constitutes ..." But Annex I and II are images; not question.
9. Notice's severability section says if exemption invalid, applicable tariff applies. Memorandum same. Fine.
10. Notice's DATES: effective July 24, but notice published July 28. It applies retroactively 4 days. That's not discrepancy but odd. Q8 tests transit exception. Memorandum signed July 23. Fine.
11. Notice at 47318 summary says "imposing tariffs on all products ... with certain exemptions as provided in Annexes I and II." But Annex I note 52(a) says additional duties apply to all products except headings 9903.05.85-9903.06.21 and subdivisions b-k. Fine.
12. Notice at 47318 says "for an economy that imposes a forced labor import prohibition... 10 percent ... with specific economies subject to a 10 percent rate net of MFN." But actual net economies are EU/Taiwan (10) and Japan/Korea/Switzerland (12.5), not necessarily economies meeting criteria? Japan/Korea/Switzerland did not impose ban/ART/partial regime, yet get net 12.5. The summary says "for an economy that imposes... 10 percent ... with specific economies subject to a 10 percent rate net of MFN" — it doesn't say all net economies meet criteria; okay.
13. Notice at 47321 says "for a product of Japan, Korea, or Switzerland ... sum ... 12.5 percent" but country-specific determination for Japan at 47324 and South Korea at 47327, Switzerland at 47327. Fine.
14. Notice at 47329-30 says "imposing distinct tariff rates on each of these groups ... would hinder" but it actually imposes 10 to all three groups; fine.
15. Notice at 47334 says "maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent" possibly conflicts with total duties >12.5 for flat countries. But "maximum tariffs" likely section 301 rate. Could be a discrepancy statement: USTR says comments fail to show disruptions "particularly with maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent" — maximum additional rate is 12.5, true. Not total.
16. Notice at 47318 says "all products ... with certain exemptions as provided in Annexes I and II." But Annex II is product exemptions; Annex I includes HTS modifications. Fine.
17. Notice at 47318 summary says "10 percent ... with specific economies subject to a 10 percent rate net of a product's MFN duty." Could imply 10% for all listed; but Japan etc. 12.5 net. It says "For every other economy ... 12.5 percent ... with specific economies subject to a 12.5 percent rate net." Fine.
18. Notice at 47319 says "Following ... additional economies have imposed forced labor import prohibitions--Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad and Tobago; or undertaken commitments ... Jordan." But June proposal already listed Cambodia and Guatemala as ART economies at 10%; not necessarily inaccurate, they additionally imposed bans.
19. Notice line 233-234: "Jordan" ART. Adopted Jordan 10%. June Jordan was 12.5 (not ART), so rate changed. Correct.
20. Notice specific determination for Canada at 47323 says "except as provided in Annex I and Annex II, Part A" but it also has Part? Canada doesn't have own part. Fine.
21. Notice specific determination for India says "except as provided in Annex I and Annex II, Part A" but India is 10% flat; no Part. Fine.
22. Notice specific determination for UK at 47328 likely 10% and Parts A and B; need check.
23. Notice specific determination for Taiwan says "Annex II, Parts A and K"; fine.
24. Notice specific determination for Switzerland "Parts A and D"; fine.
25. Notice specific determination for EU "Parts A and C"; fine.
26. Notice specific determination for Japan "Annex II, Part A" only; fine.
27. Notice specific determination for South Korea "Part A" only; fine.
28. Notice specific determination for Norway "Part A"; fine.

Potential big discrepancy: Memorandum Section 1(b)(v) includes "certain products of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, or the United Kingdom..." But adopted Annex II includes negotiated lists for these plus Taiwan etc. Fine. However memorandum says "Annex to this memorandum" while notice says Annexes I and II; not discrepancy.

Section 338:
- Original proclamations signed July 20, published July 23, effective Aug 19. Suspension signed Aug 18, published Aug 24, changes effective date to Aug 22. Later docs recitals say "effective August 19" (11061 ¶1, 11062 ¶1, 11063 ¶1, 11064 ¶1, 11065 ¶1, 11076 ¶1) despite suspension changing to Aug 22. That's a clear discrepancy: later docs describe original duties as effective August 19, while operative suspension clause sets Aug 22. But those later docs may be referring to original proclamation's stated date, not current. Q2(b) asks exactly this. Q11 should list.
- 11056 clause (1) says "effective date ... shall be 12:01 a.m. August 22. Accordingly, chapeau of Annex II of each ... amended by deleting 'August 19' and inserting 'August 22'." But it does not amend operative clauses (1)/(3) in body, which still say Aug 19. This is internal inconsistency. Later documents say duties became effective Aug 22. Q2(b) resolves via suspension clause (1) and later recitals/clauses. Q11 list.
- 11056 recitals ¶1-3 say "effective August 19" (original). Fine.
- 11061 ¶1 says original duties effective Aug 19, but ¶2 says suspension temporarily suspended 3 days, ¶4 says became effective Aug 22. Internal inconsistency within same document (¶1 vs ¶4). Same in 11062/11063/11064/11065/11076. Could list each? Q11 asks list each discrepancy once; perhaps one entry for pattern across docs, but each document different page. We can list as one pattern with multiple cites.
- 11061 clause (3) says "Besides changing certain products ... this proclamation does not otherwise affect the products, as further established in the Proclamation of September 8, 2026 (Modifying Scope... Alcoholic Beverages)..." That referenced proclamation is 11064, signed same day. Fine.
- 11062 clause (3) refers to "Proclamation of September 8, 2026 (Modifying the Scope ... Dairy)" but no such proclamation was published. This is a reference to nonexistent document. That's a discrepancy / gap. Q1 asks which docs changed dairy products; answer no dairy scope modification. Q11 list.
- 11061 footnote? Clause (3) says "as further established in the Proclamation of September 8, 2026 (Modifying the Scope ... Alcoholic Beverages)" — that's 11064, which took effect Sept 15. Fine.
- 11063 clause (3) refers to 11065; fine.
- 11064 §1 says Part A subject, Part B no longer subject; applies in addition to 232. Original 11046 clause (2) says duties shall not apply to 232 articles. The modification overrides for all? This is a change but not necessarily discrepancy.
- 11061 exclusion clause (1) effective "goods imported on or after" Sept 29, clause (2) says products "imported, but not yet entered for consumption... prior to Sept 29 remain subject to 50% duty." This creates potential gap: goods imported before Sept 29 but entered after are subject to duty, not ban. Fine.
- 11061 clause (2) says "Products that will be subject to the import ban ... that were imported, but not yet entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, prior to September 29, 2026..." The phrase "or withdrawn ... prior to" could mean if withdrawn before, but then not subject. Operative likely imported but not entered. Fine.
- 11061 clause (9)(b) says if import ban invalidated, 50% duty applies. Fine.
- 11035? No.

Need search section 338 docs for "August 19" and "August 22" to identify discrepancies.

content.text:
Clear.

Need Q1 dates published/signed all. We have. Need first page citations. Good.

Now Q10:
Scenario 1 Canadian aluminum extrusions listed Annex II of MV duty since signed, no Part A/B/exclusion. Subject 232 50% full value, entered under 9903.82.02. MFN 3%, value 200k, no USMCA.
- (a) Sept 10: MFN 6,000; 232 100,000; 338? Section 338 original Annex II, but original clause 2 excludes articles subject to 232. On Sept 10 before Sept 15 MV scope mod, so 338 = 0. Section 301? Canada 10% flat, but note 52(f) exempts aluminum articles under 9903.82.02. So 0. Total 106,000.
- (b) Sept 16: same MFN 6,000; 232 100,000; 338? After Sept 15 MV scope mod says duties as modified apply in addition to 232. Extrusion in Annex II, not Part B (no removal), so 338 50% = 100,000. Section 301 still exempt 0. Total 206,000. Need check Canada 301 10% flat and 232 exemption. Yes.
Scenario 2 Canadian rye whisky Annex II alcohol, not scope modified, Annex exclusion. MFN free, value 60k.
- (c) Sept 1, USMCA claim: Section 338? Alcohol original clause 2 excludes only 232/civil aircraft, not USMCA. 50% = 30,000. Section 301: Canada 10% but heading 9903.05.93 exempts Canadian products entered free of duty under USMCA. So 0. Total 30,000.
- (d) Sept 1 no USMCA: 338 30,000; 301 Canada 10% = 6,000. Total 36,000. (MFN free.)
- (e) arrives Oct 2: Exclusion proclamation effective Sept 29 bans importation of listed product. It may not be imported. No duty? If imported illegally, 338? Clause 2 only covers imported but not entered before Sept 29; here imported after, banned. So restriction, no lawful duty. Need answer "may not be imported; no duty computation because import prohibited." Maybeif entered, CBP would deny entry. Section 301? The product is subject to ban, but also section 301? Since exclusion from importation. Section 301 action still applies to all products of Canada not exempt; but whisky is not on section 301 exemption list? It's alcohol, likely not exempt. Does section 301 apply if 338 ban? If goods cannot be imported, no duty. But question asks 338, 301 and total for shipment arrives Oct 2. It expects import prohibition, perhaps 0 duties because no entry allowed. Need mention if somehow entered, 301 10% (6,000) might apply, but 338 ban prohibits. Hmm.

Q10(f): Client asks whether Canadian goods entered in Sept 2026 also bear IEEPA northern border duties or 10% temporary import surcharge. Need research. We saw IEEPA EOs. Need determine status by Sept 2026. Search for termination/suspension of northern border duties and temporary import surcharge. The IEEPA "northern border" duties imposed Feb/March 2025, amended. Were they terminated? Need search. "Temporary import surcharge" maybe 10% under IEEPA? Could be 2025 reciprocal tariff? Let's search.

    68  Imposing a Temporary Import Surcharge To Address 
    69                  Fundamental International Payments Problems
    70  
    71                  By the President of the United States of America
    72  
    73                  A Proclamation
    74  
    75                  1. The United States plays a pivotal role in shaping 
    76                  the global economy. At the same time, the United States 
    77                  faces various threats to its own economy and national 
    78                  interests. Sometimes, the United States faces 
    79                  fundamental international payments problems, such as 
    80                  large and serious balance-of-payments deficits, an 
    81                  imminent and significant depreciation of its currency 
    82                  in foreign exchange markets, or an international 
    83                  balance-of-payments disequilibrium. These problems can, 
    84                  among other things, endanger the ability of the United 
    85                  States to finance its spending, erode investor 
    86                  confidence in the economy, and distress the financial 
    87                  markets.
    88  
    89                  2. Special import measures to restrict imports, such as 
    90                  surcharges and quotas, are key tools to protect the 
    91                  economy and national security of the United States, 
    92                  and, in certain circumstances, they are required to 
    93                  deal with fundamental international payments problems.
    94  
    95                  3. Given the gravity of fundamental international 
    96                  payments problems and the importance of import 
    97                  restrictions as economic, national security, and 
    98                  foreign policy tools, Federal law, including section 
    99                  122 of the Trade Act of 1974 (19 U.S.C. 2132) (section 
   100                  122), empowers the President to take action through 
   101                  surcharges and other special import restrictions to 
   102                  address fundamental international payments problems.
   103  
   104                  4. I have received certain requested information and 
   105                  opinions from senior officials on whether any 
   106                  fundamental international payments problems exist and 
   107                  the extent to which such problems could impair United 
   108                  States national interests, including economic and 
   109                  national security interests. The information and 
   110                  opinions discuss, among other things, the state of the

Good. For Sept 2026 no surcharge. IEEPA duties ended Feb 20, 2026, no longer collected. Need also check original northern border EO rates and dates for Q15 historical entries. Q15 requires every additional duty on Canadian aluminum extrusions at many dates, including IEEPA duties 2025, temporary surcharge 2026, section 232, section 338, section 301. Need detailed timeline.

Q15 is complex. Need read all Canada IEEPA EOs/amendments and section 232 proclamations (April 2026 aluminum/steel/copper, June 2026 modification), plus any Canada-specific 232 duties? It says extrusions are aluminum article within section 232 aluminum duties, in 2026 listed in Annex I-A of April proclamation and not Annex I-C of June. Need know rates/dates. We need research 2025-2026 Canada tariffs.

Let's break Q15:
Entry dates:
1 Feb 10 2025
2 Mar 6 2025
3 Mar 10 2025
4 Mar 14 2025
5 Jun 3 2025
6 Jun 10 2025
7 Aug 5 2025
8 Mar 2 2026
9 Jun 10 2026
10 Jul 27 2026
11 Aug 25 2026
12 Sep 14 2026
13 Sep 16 2026
14 Nov 10 2026

Need every additional duty legally owed in addition to MFN, by authority, amount, total, and for each other additional duty then in force on Canadian products say why not owed. Cases N (no USMCA) and U (USMCA claim).

Goods: aluminum extrusions (bars, rods, profiles 7604) product of Canada, all aluminum, value 100k. Section 232 aluminum article. From April 6, 2026 entered under 9903.82.02. Before that? Section 232 aluminum duties existing from 2018 at 10%, then 25% in 2025? Need details. The prompt says "Assume that throughout the period the extrusions are an aluminum article within the section 232 aluminum duties (in 2026, listed in Annex I-A of the April proclamation on aluminum, steel and copper and not in Annex I-C of the June proclamation); that they have been listed in Annex II of the section 338 motor-vehicles duty proclamation since it was signed and are on no Part A, Part B or exclusion list; that no reduction granted to a particular producer or under an approved plan applies; and that no exemption exists other than those readable as text. From April 6, 2026 the extrusions are entered under section 232 heading 9903.82.02."

We need section 232 rates over time. Likely March 2025 aluminum duty increased to 25%. Need find proclamations. Search.

content.text:
Read 2025 aluminum proclamation and June 2025, then 2026 April/June. Need rates and effective dates, USMCA exemptions, derivative inclusion. Q15 has extrusions 7604, likely aluminum derivative? In 2025, 7604 is aluminum article subject to 25%? Need confirm. The scenario assumes "aluminum article within section 232 aluminum duties" throughout, so rate from proclamations. Perhaps 25% from March 12, 2025. Q15 dates:
Feb 10, 2025: before 25% effective March 12. Original 10% aluminum duty? Proclamation 10895 may increase from 10 to 25 effective March 12, 2025. On Feb 10, 10% still.
Mar 6: 10% (before Mar 12).
Mar 10: 10%.
Mar 14: 25%.
Jun 3: 25% before June 4 increase to 50%? June 2025 proclamation 10947 signed June 3, effective June 4 2025, raises to 50%. Need check.
Jun 10: 50%.
Aug 5: 50%.
Mar 2 2026: 50% still? April 2026 changes to 50% perhaps with new regime effective April 6. Need check.
Jun 10 2026: April proclamation maybe 50%, June proclamation changes rates? It may create 50% on full value, with 25% on derivatives? Need read.
Jul 27 2026: July 20 aluminum proclamation maybe raises to 50%? Already 50.
Aug 25, Sep 14, Sep 16, Nov 10: 50%.

But Q15 asks "every additional duty in addition to MFN" including IEEPA Canada 25% in 2025, temporary 10% surcharge in 2026, section 338, section 301. Need map dates.

Let's read 2025 aluminum proclamation 10895.

    69  
    70                  By the President of the United States of America
    71  
    72                  A Proclamation
    73  
    74                  1. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce 
    75                  (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on his 
    76                  investigation into the effect of imports of aluminum on 
    77                  the national security of the United States under 
    78                  section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as 
    79                  amended (19 U.S.C. 1862) (section 232). The Secretary 
    80                  found and advised me of the Secretary's opinion that 
    81                  aluminum is being imported into the United States in 
    82                  such quantities and under such circumstances as to 
    83                  threaten to impair the national security of the United 
    84                  States.
    85  
    86                  2. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    87                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), I 
    88                  concurred in the Secretary's finding that aluminum was 
    89                  being imported into the United States in such 
    90                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    91                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    92                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    93                  by imposing a 10 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    94                  articles imported from most countries. Proclamation 
    95                  9704 further stated that any country with which the 
    96                  United States has a security relationship is welcome to 
    97                  discuss alternative ways to address the threatened 
    98                  impairment of the national security caused by imports 
    99                  from that country, and noted that, should the United 
   100                  States and any such country arrive at a satisfactory 
   101                  alternative means to address the threat to the national 
   102                  security such that I determine that imports from that 
   103                  country no longer threaten to impair the national 
   104                  security, I may remove or modify the restriction on 
   105                  aluminum articles imports from that country and, if 
   106                  necessary, adjust the tariff as it applies to other 
   107                  countries, as the national security interests of the 
   108                  United States require.
   109  
   110                  3. In Proclamation 9704, I also directed the Secretary 
   111                  to monitor imports of aluminum articles and inform me 
   112                  of any circumstances that in the Secretary's opinion 
   113                  might indicate the need for further action under 
   114                  section 232 with respect to such imports. Pursuant to 
   115                  Proclamation 9704, the Secretary was authorized to 
   116                  provide relief from the additional duties, based on a 
   117                  request from a directly affected party located in the 
   118                  United States, for any aluminum article determined not 
   119                  to be produced in the United States in a sufficient and 
   120                  reasonably available amount or of a satisfactory 
   121                  quality, or based upon specific national security 
   122                  considerations. Proclamation 9776 of August 29, 2018, 
   123                  and Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020, similarly 
   124                  authorized the Secretary to provide relief from certain 
   125                  tariffs on other aluminum products and derivatives set 
   126                  forth in those proclamations.
   127  
   128                  4. In subsequent proclamations, the President adjusted 
   129                  the tariffs applicable to aluminum articles imports 
   130                  from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, the European 
   131                  Union (EU), and the United Kingdom (UK), after engaging 
   132                  in discussions with each of those parties on 
   133                  alternative ways to address the threat to the national 
   134                  security from such imports.
   135  
   136                  5. The Secretary has informed me that, notwithstanding 
   137                  the 10 percent ad valorem tariff imposed by 
   138                  Proclamation 9704 that mitigated the threatened 
   139                  impairment of our national security, aluminum imports 
   140                  into the United States have continued at unacceptable 
   141                  levels as the global aluminum excess capacity crisis 
   142                  continues. In addition, the exclusion of certain 
   143                  countries
   144  
   145  [[Page 9808]]
   146  
   147                  and products from the tariff and efforts by foreign 
   148                  producers to circumvent the tariff have undermined the 
   149                  purpose of Proclamation 9704, which was to adjust the 
   150                  level of imports of aluminum to remove the threatened 
   151                  impairment of the national security. This has again 
   152                  resulted in aluminum smelter capacity utilization rates 
   153                  in the domestic aluminum industry that are well below 
   154                  the target level recommended in the Secretary's January 
   155                  19, 2018, report. This indicates that the initial 
   156                  tariff of 10 percent ad valorem is not high enough to 
   157                  address the threatened impairment to our national 
   158                  security posed by aluminum imports.
   159  
   160                  6. In particular, the Secretary has informed me that 
   161                  global primary aluminum capacity has continued to 
   162                  increase, fueled by expansions in the People's Republic 
   163                  of China (China) and South America, which is seen in 
   164                  rising aluminum imports that continue to weigh on the 
   165                  price domestic aluminum producers may charge. There has 
   166                  also been a significant increase in Chinese investment 
   167                  in Mexico, driven by massive Chinese government 
   168                  subsidies and the continued ability to exploit 
   169                  loopholes in U.S. trade policy.
   170  
   171                  7. Domestic aluminum producers have been forced to idle 
   172                  additional production and shut down facilities. Two 
   173                  primary aluminum smelters within the United States have 
   174                  closed since Proclamation 9704 was promulgated. In 
   175                  addition, U.S. primary aluminum production decreased by 
   176                  30 percent from 2020 to 2024, and U.S. smelter capacity 
   177                  utilization was only 52 percent in 2024. Overcapacity 
   178                  for primary aluminum has harmed downstream aluminum 
   179                  producers, including producers of aluminum extrusions 
   180                  and aluminum sheet. To allow U.S. aluminum producers to 
   181                  restart production and to incentivize new capacity, 
   182                  additional adjustments to section 232 tariffs on 
   183                  aluminum need to be made, including limiting exemptions 
   184                  and increasing the tariff rate.
   185  
   186                  8. The Secretary has informed me that imports of 
   187                  aluminum articles from countries that are excluded from 
   188                  the tariff regime or have alternative arrangements have 
   189                  remained significantly elevated at levels that once 
   190                  again threaten to impair the national security of the 
   191                  United States. The volume of U.S. imports of aluminum 
   192                  articles from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, EU 
   193                  countries, and the UK in 2024 was approximately 14 
   194                  percent higher than the average volume of such imports 
   195                  in 2015 through 2017. In particular, the volume of U.S. 
   196                  imports of primary aluminum from Canada in 2024 was 
   197                  approximately 18 percent higher than the average volume 
   198                  for 2015 through 2017. Notwithstanding Proclamation 
   199                  10782 of July 10, 2024, which imposed higher tariffs on 
   200                  certain aluminum imports from Mexico, imports of 
   201                  aluminum from Mexico have continued to surge beyond 
   202                  historical volumes. The volume of U.S. imports of 
   203                  aluminum articles from Mexico in 2024 was approximately 
   204                  35 percent higher than the average volume for 2015 
   205                  through 2017. Proclamation 10782 did not resolve the 
   206                  surge of imports of aluminum from Mexico. Mexican 
   207                  producers are using unfair trade to gain market share 
   208                  in the United States and are leveraging their access to 
   209                  unfairly traded global primary aluminum to do so. I 
   210                  understand that Mexican producers are commingling 
   211                  primary aluminum from China and the Russian Federation 
   212                  (Russia) with primary aluminum from other countries to 
   213                  produce downstream aluminum articles. These practices 
   214                  are distortive and provide continued outlets to absorb 
   215                  the massive amount of global excess capacity and must 
   216                  be remedied. The volume of U.S. imports of primary 
   217                  aluminum from Australia has also surged and in 2024 was 
   218                  approximately 103 percent higher than the average 
   219                  volume for 2015 through 2017. Australia has disregarded 
   220                  its verbal commitment to voluntarily restrain its 
   221                  aluminum exports to a reasonable level.
   222  
   223                  9. These volume increases occurred even though demand 
   224                  for aluminum in the United States and Canada (the 
   225                  market measured by industry) has generally remained 
   226                  flat, averaging about 20 percent since 2018.
   227  
   228                  10. These increasing import volumes support the 
   229                  conclusion that aluminum producers in countries subject 
   230                  to the additional ad valorem tariff proclaimed in 
   231                  Proclamation 9704 are engaging in transshipment or 
   232                  further processing
   233  
   234  [[Page 9809]]
   235  
   236                  of upstream aluminum products in countries that have 
   237                  since been exempted from that tariff. Foreign producers 
   238                  have shifted assembly or manufacturing operations to 
   239                  third countries, such as Mexico. For example, Chinese 
   240                  producers are using Mexico's general exclusion from the 
   241                  tariff to funnel Chinese aluminum to the United States 
   242                  through Mexico while avoiding the tariff.
   243  
   244                  11. The Secretary has informed me that producers in 
   245                  countries that remain subject to the ad valorem tariff 
   246                  have continued to evade the tariff by processing 
   247                  covered aluminum articles into additional downstream 
   248                  derivative products that were not included in the 
   249                  additional ad valorem tariffs proclaimed in 
   250                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9980. Foreign 
   251                  producers are continuing to expand downstream 
   252                  production to absorb the global excess capacity. 
   253                  Imports of additional derivative aluminum products have 
   254                  increased significantly since the issuance of 
   255                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9980, eroding the 
   256                  domestic industry's customer base and resulting in 
   257                  depressed demand for aluminum articles produced in the 
   258                  United States.
   259  
   260                  12. The Secretary has also informed me of the impact of 
   261                  the product exclusion process authorized by 
   262                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9776, and Proclamation 
   263                  9980 and implemented by subsequent regulations. This 
   264                  process has resulted in exclusions for a significant 
   265                  volume of imports, in a manner that undermines the 
   266                  purpose of the section 232 measures and threatens to 
   267                  impair the national security of the United States. 
   268                  Certain general approved exclusions remain in effect 
   269                  for entire tariff lines of aluminum imports, 
   270                  notwithstanding the domestic industry's potential to 
   271                  produce many excluded products.
   272  
   273                  13. I determine that these developments and 
   274                  modifications to the original tariff regime as 
   275                  proclaimed in Proclamation 9704 have undermined the 
   276                  regime's national security objectives by preventing the 
   277                  domestic aluminum industry (including derivatives) from 
   278                  achieving sustained production capacity utilization of 
   279                  at least 80 percent, as determined in the Secretary's 
   280                  January 19, 2018, report. I also determine that the 
   281                  modifications failed to achieve their articulated 
   282                  objectives. As a result, I determine that these 
   283                  modifications have resulted in significantly increasing 
   284                  imports of aluminum articles that once again threaten 
   285                  to impair the national security of the United States.
   286  
   287                  14. In light of the Secretary's findings, I have 
   288                  determined that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   289                  adjust the tariff proclaimed by Proclamation 9704, as 
   290                  amended, and the tariff proclaimed by Proclamation 
   291                  9980, as amended, to increase the tariff rate from 10 
   292                  percent ad valorem to 25 percent ad valorem. These 
   293                  actions are necessary and appropriate to remove the 
   294                  threatened impairment of the national security of the 
   295                  United States.
   296  
   297                  15. In light of the Secretary's findings regarding the 
   298                  alternative agreements with Argentina proclaimed in 
   299                  Proclamation 9758 of May 31, 2018; Australia proclaimed 
   300                  in Proclamation 9758; Canada proclaimed in Proclamation 
   301                  9893 of May 19, 2019, and Proclamation 10106 of October 
   302                  27, 2020; Mexico proclaimed in Proclamation 9893 and 
   303                  Proclamation 10782 of July 10, 2024; the European Union 
   304                  proclaimed in Proclamation 10327 of December 27, 2021, 
   305                  and Proclamation 10690 of December 28, 2023; and the 
   306                  United Kingdom proclaimed in Proclamation 10405 of May 
   307                  31, 2022, I have decided that it is necessary to 
   308                  terminate these agreements as of March 12, 2025. As of

    67                  imports of steel articles and derivative steel articles 
    68                  by imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    69                  articles imported from all countries.

    72                  a report on the Secretary's investigation into the 
    73                  effect of imports of aluminum articles on the national 
    74                  security of the United States under section 232. The 
    75                  Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that 
    76                  aluminum articles are being imported into the United 
    77                  States in such quantities and under such circumstances 
    78                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
    79                  United States.

    81                  4. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    82                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), and 
    83                  Proclamation 9980, I concurred with the Secretary's 
    84                  findings that aluminum articles, as defined in clause 1 
    85                  of Proclamation 9704, and derivative aluminum articles, 
    86                  as described in clause 3 of Proclamation 9980, are 
    87                  being imported into the United States in such 
    88                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    89                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    90                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    91                  and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 10 
    92                  percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    93                  from most countries. In Proclamation 10895 of February 
    94                  10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Aluminum Into the United 
    95                  States), I decided to adjust the imports of aluminum 
    96                  articles and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 
    97                  25 percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    98                  from all countries.

   100                  5. In Proclamation 10896 and Proclamation 10895, I 
   101                  instructed the Secretary to continue to monitor imports 
   102                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   103                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   104                  respectively, and
   105  
   106  [[Page 24200]]
   107  
   108                  to review the status of such imports with respect to 
   109                  the national security of the United States. The 
   110                  Secretary has done so and has advised me accordingly.
   111  
   112                  6. After considering current information newly provided 
   113                  by the Secretary, among other things, I have determined 
   114                  that it is necessary to increase the previously 
   115                  described steel and aluminum tariffs to adjust the 
   116                  imports of steel and aluminum articles and their 
   117                  derivative articles so that such imports will not 
   118                  threaten to impair the national security. In my 
   119                  judgment, the increased tariffs will more effectively 
   120                  counter foreign countries that continue to offload low-
   121                  priced, excess steel and aluminum in the United States 
   122                  market and thereby undercut the competitiveness of the 
   123                  United States steel and aluminum industries. Although 
   124                  the previously imposed steel and aluminum tariffs have 
   125                  helped provide critical price support in the United 
   126                  States market, they have not yet enabled these 
   127                  industries to develop and maintain the rates of 
   128                  capacity production utilization that are necessary for 
   129                  the industries' sustained health and for projected 
   130                  national defense needs. I have determined that 
   131                  increasing the previously imposed tariffs will provide 
   132                  greater support to these industries and reduce or 
   133                  eliminate the national security threat posed by imports 
   134                  of steel and aluminum articles and their derivative 
   135                  articles.

   137                  7. Accordingly, I have determined that it is necessary 
   138                  and appropriate to increase the tariff rate for imports 
   139                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   140                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   141                  from 25 percent ad valorem to 50 percent ad valorem 
   142                  effective as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   143                  June 4, 2025. I have also determined that it is 
   144                  necessary and appropriate to modify the way in which 
   145                  the tariff measures described in Executive Order 14289 
   146                  of April 29, 2025 (Addressing Certain Tariffs on 
   147                  Imported Articles), apply to steel articles and 
   148                  derivative steel articles, and aluminum articles and 
   149                  derivative aluminum articles, to ensure the 
   150                  effectiveness of the tariff changes described in this 
   151                  proclamation and the alignment of policy priorities 
   152                  between this proclamation and Executive Order 14289. I 
   153                  have further determined that it is necessary and 
   154                  appropriate to allow for the implementation of the 
   155                  U.S.-UK Economic Prosperity Deal of May 8, 2025 (EPD), 
   156                  and to accordingly provide different treatment, as 
   157                  described below, for imports of steel and aluminum 
   158                  articles, and their derivatives, from the United 
   159                  Kingdom.

   162                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   163                  being imported into the United States in such 
   164                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   165                  to impair the national security.

   168                  U.S.C. 2483), authorizes the President to embody in the 
   169                  Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) 
   170                  the substance of statutes affecting import treatment,

   176                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   177                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States 
   178                  of America, including section 232; the International 
   179                  Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.); 
   180                  section 301 of title 3, United States Code; and section 
   181                  604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended, do hereby 
   182                  proclaim as follows:

   185                  proclamation, as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   186                  June 4, 2025, the tariffs proclaimed by Proclamation 
   187                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; 
   188                  Proclamation 9980, as amended; Proclamation 10895; and 
   189                  Proclamation 10896 are modified to increase the 
   190                  respective tariff rates from an additional 25 percent 
   191                  ad valorem to an additional 50 percent ad valorem.

   193                  of this proclamation shall be effective with respect to 
   194                  goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from 
   195                  warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. 
   196                  eastern

   200                  daylight time on June 4, 2025, and shall continue in 
   201                  effect, unless such actions are expressly reduced, 
   202                  modified, or terminated.

   204                  to this proclamation that were admitted into a United 
   205                  States foreign trade zone under ``privileged foreign 
   206                  status'' as defined in 19 CFR 146.41 before 12:01 a.m. 
   207                  eastern daylight time on June 4, 2025, shall be subject 
   208                  upon entry for consumption made on or after 12:01 a.m. 
   209                  eastern daylight time on June 4, 2025, to the 
   210                  provisions of the tariff in effect at the time of the 
   211                  entry for consumption.

   213                  proclamation, except those eligible for admission under 
   214                  ``domestic status'' as defined in 19 CFR 146.43, that

   244                  Goods Trade Deficits), as amended, and any other

   252                  declaration requirements for steel and aluminum content 
   253                  in imported articles and outlining maximum penalties

   257                  monetary penalties, loss of import privileges, and 
   258                  criminal liability, consistent with United States law.

   260                  the applicable rates of duty for articles of the United 
   261                  Kingdom that would otherwise be applicable pursuant to 
   262                  Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as 
   263                  amended; Proclamation 9980, as amended; Proclamation 
   264                  10895; and Proclamation 10896 shall remain at 25 
   265                  percent ad valorem. On or after July 9, 2025, the 
   266                  Secretary may adjust the applicable rates of duty and

   268                  consistent with the terms of the EPD, or he may 
   269                  increase the applicable rates of duty to 50 percent if 
   270                  he determines that the United Kingdom has not complied 
   271                  with relevant aspects of the EPD.

   273                  of the articles and derivative articles described in 
   274                  Annexes I and II to this proclamation, and shall, from 
   275                  time to time, in consultation with any senior executive 
   276                  branch officials the Secretary deems appropriate,

   278                  national security of the United States. The Secretary

   287                  opinion, might indicate that the duty rate provided for

   289                  pursuant thereto, is no longer necessary.

   291                  the duties imposed pursuant to this proclamation.

   293                  guidance consistent with this proclamation, including

   296                  States International Trade Commission and CBP, shall 
   297                  determine whether any modifications to the HTSUS are 
   298                  necessary to effectuate this proclamation and may make 
   299                  such modifications through notice in the Federal

Important: April 2026 sets 50% full customs value for Annex I-A aluminum/steel articles, effective April 6. Extrusions in Annex I-A => 50% on full value. Before April 6, 50% on aluminum content. Since all value aluminum, same.

Need Canada exemption? Clause 10/11 likely USMCA? Let's read around 430-560.

content.text:
No change to 50% for extrusions; onshoring only. Good.

Now IEEPA northern border timeline. Need read EO 14193 and amendments to know rates/dates and USMCA exemptions. Q15 includes dates Feb 10, Mar 6, Mar 10, Mar 14, Jun 3, Jun 10, Aug 5, 2025. Need exact IEEPA duty:
- EO 14193 signed Feb 1, effective Feb 4? It imposed 25% on all Canada imports except energy 10%, but paused for 30 days until March 4. Then "Progress" EO Feb 3 paused until March 4. Amendment March 2 perhaps ended pause and set March 4. Amendment March 6 delayed some until April 2. Need read.
- At Feb 10, 2025: Duties not in effect (paused). So no IEEPA.
- Mar 6: likely 25% in effect since Mar 4? Or some paused? Need exact.
- Mar 10: 25%.
- Mar 14: 25%.
- Jun 3: 25% (unless USMCA compliant exemption from March 6 amendment? It exempted USMCA-qualifying goods). Need read.
- Jun 10: 25%.
- Aug 5: 25% (maybe increased to 35% Aug 1? Amendment July 31: 35% on non-USMCA goods effective Aug 1? Need read).
Need also "10% temporary import surcharge" from Feb 24 to July 24 2026. On Mar 2 2026, IEEPA duties ended Feb 20, surcharge applies 10% (unless Annex exceptions; aluminum articles subject to 232 exempt). So on Mar 2 2026, aluminum extrusions subject to 232 are exempt from surcharge, so no surcharge. On Jun 10 2026: surcharge still in effect until July 24, but aluminum subject to 232 exempt. So no surcharge. On Jul 27 2026: surcharge expired July 24. Thus for all dates, temporary surcharge not owed because either expired or 232 exemption. But Q15 asks "for each other additional duty then in force on products of Canada, say in a line why it is not owed." Need mention IEEPA ended Feb 20, 2026; temporary surcharge exempt because 232 (and expired after July 24). Section 338 and 301 need map.

Section 338 on extrusions: Listed Annex II of motor vehicles duty proclamation since signed (July 20, 2026), effective Aug 22 (after suspension). So for dates before Aug 22, 2026 no 338. For Aug 25, Sep 14, Sep 16, Nov 10: 338 applies? Original clause 2 excludes articles subject to 232. But MV scope modification effective Sept 15 says duties as modified apply in addition to section 232. Extrusions are in original Annex II, not Part A/B. Before Sept 15, no 338 due 232 exclusion. From Sept 15, 338 applies in addition to 232 for all remaining MV Annex II products. So:
- Aug 25, 2026: 338 no (232 exclusion).
- Sep 14: 338 no (before Sept 15).
- Sep 16: 338 yes 50% = 50,000.
- Nov 10: 338 yes 50% = 50,000 (assuming not removed by Oct 30 Part A; scenario says no Part A/B).
Section 301: Canada 10% flat, but note 52(f)(1) exempts aluminum articles of heading 9903.82.02. So 0 on all dates after July 24, 2026. Before July 24 no section 301. Good.
Section 232 rate:
- Feb 10 2025: 10%? Wait 10% aluminum tariff from 2018, but Canada had exemption/alternative arrangement until March 12, 2025. Important! Proclamation 10895 terminated Canada agreement as of March 12, 2025. Before March 12, Canadian aluminum was exempt from section 232 (via Proclamation 9893/10106). Q15 scenario says "Assume that throughout the period the extrusions are an aluminum article within the section 232 aluminum duties..." Does that mean they are subject to 232 throughout, overriding exemptions? It says "in 2026, listed in Annex I-A ... and not Annex I-C". It might assume 232 duty applies throughout, but Canada had exemption before March 12, 2025. The prompt says "Assume that throughout the period the extrusions are an aluminum article within the section 232 aluminum duties ...; ... no reduction granted to a particular producer or under an approved plan applies; and no exemption exists other than those readable as text." This likely means we must apply Canada exemptions in text. Before March 12, 2025, Canada was exempt from aluminum 232 duties by Proclamation 9893 etc. But are those "exemptions readable as text"? They are referenced in Proclamation 10895 but not the full text. Hmm.

Q15 entry dates specifically include Feb 10, Mar 6, Mar 10, 2025—before March 12—to test that Canadian aluminum was exempt under section 232 until March 12, 2025. The assumption "throughout the period the extrusions are an aluminum article within the section 232 aluminum duties" could mean they fall within the article scope, not necessarily that duty is owed. They say "no exemption exists other than those readable as text." Proclamation 10895 clause 1 terminates Canada agreement effective March 12, and recitals reference Proclamation 9893. That may be enough to know pre-March 12 Canada exempt. But we might need the actual Canada exemption proclamation text to confirm. Search Proclamation 9893 not in 2025 FR (2019). Tool only 2025-2026? It searches Federal Register likely all dates. But prompt says don't rely on memory; can search. Let's search "Proclamation 9893" or "Canada aluminum exemption".

    62  Adjusting Imports of Aluminum Into the United 
    63                  States
    64  
    65                  By the President of the United States of America
    66  
    67                  A Proclamation
    68  
    69                  1. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce 
    70                  (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on his 
    71                  investigation into the effect of imports of aluminum 
    72                  articles on the national security of the United States 
    73                  under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, 
    74                  as amended (19 U.S.C. 1862). The Secretary found and 
    75                  advised me of his opinion that aluminum articles were 
    76                  being imported into the United States in such 
    77                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    78                  to impair the national security of the United States.
    79  
    80                  2. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    81                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), I 
    82                  concurred in the Secretary's finding that aluminum 
    83                  articles were being imported into the United States in 
    84                  such quantities and under such circumstances as to 
    85                  threaten to impair the national security of the United 
    86                  States, and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum 
    87                  articles, as defined in clause 1 of Proclamation 9704, 
    88                  by imposing a 10 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    89                  articles imported from most countries.
    90  
    91                  3. In Proclamation 9704, I further stated that any 
    92                  country with which we have a security relationship is 
    93                  welcome to discuss with the United States alternative 
    94                  ways to address the threatened impairment of the 
    95                  national security caused by imports from that country, 
    96                  and noted that, should the United States and any such 
    97                  country arrive at a satisfactory alternative means to 
    98                  address the threat to the national security such that I 
    99                  determine that imports from that country no longer 
   100                  threaten to impair the national security, I may remove 
   101                  or modify the restriction on aluminum articles imports 
   102                  from that country and, if necessary, adjust the tariff 
   103                  as it applies to other countries, as the national 
   104                  security interests of the United States require.
   105  
   106                  4. The United States has successfully concluded 
   107                  discussions with Canada and Mexico on satisfactory 
   108                  alternative means to address the threatened impairment 
   109                  of the national security posed by aluminum imports from 
   110                  Canada and Mexico. The United States has agreed on a 
   111                  range of measures with Canada and Mexico to prevent the 
   112                  importation of aluminum that is unfairly subsidized or 
   113                  sold at dumped prices, to prevent the transshipment of 
   114                  aluminum, and to monitor for and avoid import surges. 
   115                  These measures are expected to allow imports of 
   116                  aluminum from Canada and Mexico to remain stable at 
   117                  historical levels without meaningful increases, thus 
   118                  permitting the domestic capacity utilization to remain 
   119                  reasonably commensurate with the target level 
   120                  recommended in the Secretary's report. In my judgment, 
   121                  these measures will provide effective, long-term 
   122                  alternative means to address the contribution of these 
   123                  countries' imports to the threatened impairment of the 
   124                  national security.
   125  
   126                  5. In light of these agreements, I have determined 
   127                  that, under the framework in the agreements, imports of 
   128                  aluminum from Canada and Mexico will no longer threaten 
   129                  to impair the national security, and thus I have 
   130                  decided to exclude Canada and Mexico from the tariff 
   131                  proclaimed in Proclamation 9704, as amended. The United 
   132                  States will monitor the implementation and 
   133                  effectiveness of these measures in addressing our 
   134                  national security needs, and I may revisit this 
   135                  determination as appropriate.
   136  
   137  [[Page 23984]]
   138  
   139                  6. In light of my determination to exclude, on a long-
   140                  term basis, these countries from the tariff proclaimed 
   141                  in Proclamation 9704, as amended, I have considered 
   142                  whether it is necessary and appropriate in light of our 
   143                  national security interests to make any corresponding 
   144                  adjustments to such tariff as it applies to other 
   145                  countries. I have determined that, in light of the 
   146                  agreed-upon measures with Canada and Mexico, it is 
   147                  necessary and appropriate, at this time, to maintain 
   148                  the current tariff level as it applies to other 
   149                  countries.
   150  
   151                  7. Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as 
   152                  amended, authorizes the President to adjust the imports 
   153                  of an article and its derivatives that are being 
   154                  imported into the United States in such quantities or 
   155                  under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the 
   156                  national security.
   157  
   158                  8. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
   159                  U.S.C. 2483), authorizes the President to embody in the 
   160                  Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) 
   161                  the substance of statutes affecting import treatment, 
   162                  and actions thereunder, including the removal, 
   163                  modification, continuance, or imposition of any rate of 
   164                  duty or other import restriction.
   165  
   166                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   167                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   168                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States 
   169                  of America, including section 232 of the Trade 
   170                  Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, section 301 of title 
   171                  3, United States Code, and section 604 of the Trade Act 
   172                  of 1974, as amended, do hereby proclaim as follows:
   173  
   174                      (1) Clause 2 of Proclamation 9704, as amended, is 
   175                  further amended in the second sentence by deleting the 
   176                  ``and'' before ``(c)'' and inserting before the period 
   177                  at the end: ``, and (d) on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern 
   178                  daylight time on May 20, 2019, from all countries 
   179                  except Argentina, Australia, Canada, and Mexico''.
   180                      (2) The ``Article description'' for heading 
   181                  9903.85.01, in subchapter III of chapter 99 of the 
   182                  HTSUS, is amended by replacing ``of Australia'' with 
   183                  ``of Australia, of Canada, of Mexico''.
   184                      (3) The modifications made by clauses 1 and 2 of 
   185                  this proclamation shall be effective with respect to 
   186                  goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from 
   187                  warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. 
   188                  eastern daylight time on May 20, 2019, and shall 
   189                  continue in effect, unless such actions are expressly 
   190                  reduced, modified, or terminated.
   191                      (4) Any imports of aluminum articles from Canada 
   192                  and Mexico that were admitted into a U.S. foreign trade 
   193                  zone under ``privileged foreign status'' as defined in 
   194                  19 CFR 146.41, prior to 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight 
   195                  time on May 20, 2019, shall not be subject upon entry 
   196                  for consumption made after 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight 
   197                  time on May 20, 2019, to the additional 10 percent ad 
   198                  valorem rate of duty imposed by Proclamation 9704, as 
   199                  amended.
   200                      (5) Any provision of previous proclamations and 
   201                  Executive Orders that is inconsistent with the actions 
   202                  taken in this proclamation is superseded to the extent 
   203                  of such inconsistency.

    27                  Executive Order 14193 of February 1, 2025
    28  
    29                  
    30  Imposing Duties To Address the Flow of Illicit 
    31                  Drugs Across Our Northern Border
    32  
    33                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    34                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    35                  America, including the International Emergency Economic 
    36                  Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) (IEEPA), the 
    37                  National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.) 
    38                  (NEA), section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended 
    39                  (19 U.S.C. 2483), and section 301 of title 3, United 
    40                  States Code,
    41  
    42                  I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of 
    43                  America, find that the sustained influx of illicit 
    44                  opioids and other drugs has profound consequences on 
    45                  our Nation, endangering lives and putting a severe 
    46                  strain on our healthcare system, public services, and 
    47                  communities.
    48  
    49                  This challenge threatens the fabric of our society. 
    50                  Gang members, smugglers, human traffickers, and illicit 
    51                  drugs of all kinds have poured across our borders and 
    52                  into our communities. Canada has played a central role 
    53                  in these challenges, including by failing to devote 
    54                  sufficient attention and resources or meaningfully 
    55                  coordinate with United States law enforcement partners 
    56                  to effectively stem the tide of illicit drugs.
    57  
    58                  Drug trafficking organizations (DTOs) are the world's 
    59                  leading producers of fentanyl, methamphetamine, 
    60                  cocaine, and other illicit drugs, and they cultivate, 
    61                  process, and distribute massive quantities of narcotics 
    62                  that fuel addiction and violence in communities across 
    63                  the United States. These DTOs often collaborate with 
    64                  transnational cartels to smuggle illicit drugs into the 
    65                  United States, utilizing clandestine airstrips, 
    66                  maritime routes, and overland corridors.
    67  
    68                  The challenges at our southern border are foremost in 
    69                  the public consciousness, but our northern border is 
    70                  not exempt from these issues. Criminal networks are 
    71                  implicated in human trafficking and smuggling 
    72                  operations, enabling unvetted illegal migration across 
    73                  our northern border. There is also a growing presence 
    74                  of Mexican cartels operating fentanyl and nitazene 
    75                  synthesis labs in Canada. The flow of illicit drugs 
    76                  like fentanyl to the United States through both illicit 
    77                  distribution networks and international mail--due, in 
    78                  the case of the latter, to the existing administrative 
    79                  exemption from duty and taxes, also known as de 
    80                  minimis, under section 1321 of title 19, United States 
    81                  Code--has created a public health crisis in the United 
    82                  States, as outlined in the Presidential Memorandum of 
    83                  January 20, 2025 (America First Trade Policy) and 
    84                  Executive Order 14157 of January 20, 2025 (Designating 
    85                  Cartels and Other Organizations as Foreign Terrorist 
    86                  Organizations and Specially Designated Global 
    87                  Terrorists). With respect to smuggling of illicit drugs 
    88                  across our northern border, Canada's Financial 
    89                  Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre recently 
    90                  published a study on the laundering of proceeds of 
    91                  illicit synthetic opioids, which recognized Canada's 
    92                  heightened domestic production of fentanyl, largely 
    93                  from British Columbia, and its growing footprint within 
    94                  international narcotics distribution. Despite a North 
    95                  American dialogue on the public health impacts of 
    96                  illicit drugs since 2016, Canadian officials have 
    97                  acknowledged that the problem has only grown. And while 
    98                  U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) within the 
    99                  Department of Homeland Security seized, comparatively, 
   100                  much less fentanyl from Canada than from Mexico last 
   101                  year, fentanyl is so potent that even a very small 
   102                  parcel of the drug can cause many deaths and
   103  
   104  [[Page 9114]]
   105  
   106                  destruction to America families. In fact, the amount of 
   107                  fentanyl that crossed the northern border last year 
   108                  could kill 9.5 million Americans.
   109  
   110                  Immediate action is required to finally end this public 
   111                  health crisis and national emergency, which will not 
   112                  happen unless the compliance and cooperation of Canada 
   113                  is assured.
   114  
   115                  I hereby determine and order:
   116  
   117                  Section 1. (a) As President of the United States, my 
   118                  highest duty is the defense of the country and its 
   119                  citizens. A Nation without borders is not a nation at 
   120                  all. I will not stand by and allow our sovereignty to 
   121                  be eroded, our laws to be trampled, our citizens to be 
   122                  endangered, or our borders to be disrespected anymore.
   123  
   124                  I previously declared a national emergency with respect 
   125                  to the grave threat to the United States posed by the 
   126                  influx of illegal aliens and illicit drugs into the 
   127                  United States in Proclamation 10886 of January 20, 2025 
   128                  (Declaring a National Emergency at the Southern 
   129                  Border). Pursuant to the NEA, I hereby expand the scope 
   130                  of the national emergency declared in that Proclamation 
   131                  to cover the threat to the safety and security of 
   132                  Americans, including the public health crisis of deaths 
   133                  due to the use of fentanyl and other illicit drugs, and 
   134                  the failure of Canada to do more to arrest, seize, 
   135                  detain, or otherwise intercept DTOs, other drug and 
   136                  human traffickers, criminals at large, and drugs. In 
   137                  addition, this failure to act on the part of Canada 
   138                  constitutes an unusual and extraordinary threat, which 
   139                  has its source in substantial part outside the United 
   140                  States, to the national security and foreign policy of 
   141                  the United States. I hereby declare and reiterate a 
   142                  national emergency under the NEA and IEEPA to deal with 
   143                  that threat. This national emergency requires decisive

    79  
    80                  Section 1. Background. In Executive Order 14193 of 
    81                  February 1, 2025 (Imposing Duties To Address the Flow 
    82                  of Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border), I 
    83                  declared a national emergency arising from certain 
    84                  conditions, including the public health crisis caused 
    85                  by fentanyl and other illicit drugs, and the failure of 
    86                  Canada to do more to arrest, seize, detain, or 
    87                  otherwise intercept drug trafficking organizations, 
    88                  other drug or human traffickers, criminals at large,

    95                  To deal with the emergency declared in Executive Order 
    96                  14193, I imposed an additional ad valorem rate of duty 
    97                  of 25 percent on certain articles that are products of 
    98                  Canada and an additional ad valorem rate of duty of 10 
    99                  percent on certain energy or energy resources that are 
   100                  products of Canada. In Executive Order 14231 of March 
   101                  6, 2025 (Amendment to Duties To Address the Flow of 
   102                  Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border), I provided 
   103                  that the additional ad valorem rates of duties under 
   104                  Executive Order 14193 do not apply to articles that are 
   105                  products of Canada that qualify for duty-free entry 
   106                  under the Agreement between the United States of 
   107                  America, United Mexican States, and Canada (USMCA), and 
   108                  I reduced the additional ad valorem rate of duty on 
   109                  potash from 25 percent to 10 percent.
   110  
   111                  Section 2(d) of Executive Order 14193 provides that 
   112                  ``[s]hould Canada retaliate against the United States . 
   113                  . . through import duties on United States exports to 
   114                  Canada or similar measures,'' I ``may increase or 
   115                  expand in scope the duties imposed . . . to ensure the 
   116                  efficacy of th[e] action'' taken in Executive Order 
   117                  14193. Section 3(b) of Executive Order 14193 provides 
   118                  that the Secretary of Homeland Security, in 
   119                  coordination with other senior officials, ``shall 
   120                  recommend additional action, if necessary, should the 
   121                  Government of Canada fail to take adequate steps to 
   122                  alleviate the illegal migration and illicit drug crises 
   123                  through cooperative enforcement actions.''
